t: a sick person who is in danger. One whose life is in danger (the definition is explained below, halachot 4-6).
an expert physician of that place. A professional physician of that city, who diagnosed the patient as being in danger of his life.
for even a doubt concerning life overrides the Sabbath. And not only rescue from a certain danger.
they assessed him. The physicians estimated his condition.
that he requires such and such for eight days. For some treatment involving work forbidden on the Sabbath, which will have to be done both on this Sabbath and on the next Sabbath.
we do not say, let us wait etc.. We do not delay treatment of a patient in danger in order to reduce Sabbath desecration.
and we heat water for him etc.. Heating water for drinking or for bathing.

it is like a weekday for everything he needs. It is considered a weekday for those needs, and there is no need to perform them with a change (unlike what is explained below, halachah 11; Maggid Mishneh).
not through gentiles etc.. For each of these there are various grounds of exemption from certain commandments.

so that the Sabbath not be taken lightly in their eyes. If the desecration of the Sabbath is handed over to them, onlookers might not understand that it is permitted for the sake of saving a life, which could lead to disrespect for the sanctity of the Sabbath (and see below 6:1).
but through the great ones of Israel. Important Torah scholars, so that it is understood that this is a special situation permitted only to save lives (and see Piskei VeShitot).
to delay. To be held up.
he shall live by them, and not die by them. The commandments are meant for life, not for people to die because of them (see also Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 5:1).
vengeance. Punishment.
the minim (heretics). Those who denied the tradition of the Sages.
and I also gave them statutes that were not good and ordinances by which they could not live. For such people the laws of the Torah do indeed serve as punishment and as a cause of death.
one who has pain in his eyes. One who has an eye disease.
discharge. Mucus.
inflammation. Inflammation.
among the sick who are in danger. For eye diseases can endanger life.
a wound in the cavity of his body. An injury to the internal organs.
the lip. The lips.
in any other internal part. The other internal organs.
assessment. A medical diagnosis of the severity of his condition (above, halachah 1).
and a wound on the back of the hand or the back of the foot. An injury on their outer side, which may cause heavy loss of blood.
and a fever that makes the flesh bristle. A fever with chills.
a thread of water. A leech found in water.
a mad dog. A dog with rabies, whose bite may be fatal.
one of the crawling creatures of the earth that kill. For example, poisonous snakes.
to bring him a single dried fig. To bring from another domain food for his cure in the quantity of a dried fig, which is the minimum quantity for liability for carrying out food (below 18:1).
for all of them brought it in a permitted domain. For the purpose of saving lives.
two dried figs. To eat two figs as a cure, which must be picked from the tree for him on the Sabbath.
by two stems. That must be picked in two separate acts.
and three dried figs by one stem. That can be picked in a single act of detaching.
so that they will not do more picking. Even though in practice more figs were picked than needed, it is preferable to minimize the forbidden acts.
and left over. Left over some of the cooked food.
a decree, lest he cook more for him. Out of concern that he might cook more than the patient needs from the outset, for another, healthy, person.
raw meat. For it is forbidden to cook it for a healthy person on the Sabbath.
for there is no addition etc.. For the slaughter is one act, whether much meat is needed or little, and here it was permitted for the sick person.
all his needs are done for him through a gentile. Since the prohibition of telling a gentile to act is a rabbinic decree (below 6:1), and they did not apply it where there is illness (ibid. 6:9).
and likewise one who applies kohl to his eyes etc.. Eye treatment with kohl powder, used as cosmetic and as an eye disinfectant. Applying kohl is forbidden on the Sabbath (below 23:12).

even though there is no danger there. Although this is not a life-threatening illness that overrides the Sabbath, because of the suffering of the illness they permitted his needs to be done through a gentile.
there is no work in them. There is no concern that these medical actions might lead to forbidden work (see below 21:31).
we set the ears. We return the lower jaw if it was dislocated.
and we set the unkali. The unkali is the protrusion of the hook, the lower end of the breastbone (the "heart's key"). If it bends inward it may press on the stomach.
and we reset the fracture. We return a broken bone to its place.
when she crouches to give birth. This state is explained below, halachah 13.
they call a midwife for her from place to place. A midwife is summoned even from a distant place.
crying out in her labor pains. Crying out because of the birth pangs, and she must be calmed.
even if she was blind. Even if the woman is blind and cannot see the light of the lamp.
for her mind is settled by a lamp. She calms down if she knows a lamp is lit.
and whatever can be done differently etc.. Bringing oil is not essential for saving life, so it is done with a change if possible.
a vessel hanging from her hair. For this is not the usual way of carrying out (see below 12:13-14).

we do not deliver a gentile woman etc.. On weekdays one may deliver a gentile woman only for pay and to avoid hostility (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 9:16); on the Sabbath this reason does not apply, since Israelites could excuse themselves and say they desecrate the Sabbath only for Sabbath observers.
a resident alien. A gentile living in the Land of Israel who accepted upon himself the seven Noahide commandments (ibid. 10:6).

commanded to keep him alive. To assist him and look after his life, as it says "a stranger and a resident, that he may live with you" (Leviticus 25:35; and see Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 3:11, Hilchot Melachim 10:10-12).
a woman who has given birth. A woman in childbirth.
from when the blood begins to flow etc.. During this time period she is considered a sick person in danger.
and if she was silent. If she did not object to work being done for her on the Sabbath.
we make a fire. We light a fire to warm the house.
for cold is harmful to a woman who has given birth. The cold weighs heavily on the woman who gave birth (see also Hilchot Shevitat Asor 3:8).
we do not make a fire for a sick person. For cold is not so harmful to an ordinary sick person who is not in danger.
he was bled and became chilled. And therefore needs to be warmed.
in the season of Tammuz. In midsummer.
we wash the newborn... even in water heated on the Sabbath. Although washing in hot water is forbidden on the Sabbath (below 22:2-3), if necessary water is even heated for him on the Sabbath.
and we salt him. A treatment given to a newborn to strengthen him.
and we wrap. Swaddle.
and likewise we wash him before the circumcision. With water heated before the Sabbath (see Hilchot Milah 2:7).

and after the circumcision... it is permitted to rinse him with water heated on the Sabbath because of danger. If after the circumcision the water prepared in advance was spilled, it is permitted even to heat water on the Sabbath because of the danger (ibid. 2:8).
who sat on the birthstool. Crouched to give birth.
even through the public domain. Where carrying an object is forbidden by the Torah.
even for this one whose presumption is not that he is alive. Who was not alive before; a mere doubt of saving a life suffices to justify desecrating the Sabbath.
we remove debris to save a life etc.. To save them from urgent danger, and one must not delay to check whether it is permitted (and see below, end of halachah 17).
a net. A net for catching fish.
even though he catches fish with it. Which involves the labor of trapping (below 10:19).
and brought up only fish, he is exempt from everything. Because he intended to rescue.
since he brought up a child with the fish, he is exempt. For he accomplished a permitted act (see also Hilchot Shegagot 2:15).
he removes a section. A piece from the edge of the pit, to allow the child to be taken out.
he makes a step with it. So he has done work to improve that pit.
for he splits it into wood fit for work. He cuts it into planks, which is the labor of cutting (below 11:7).
he will be frightened. He will be afraid.
he tramples a road and prepares it. In the course of breaking in, he tramples down a new path and makes it fit for walking, which is a derivative of the labor of plowing (below 8:1).
we clear debris for him. We remove the stones of the collapse to free him.
they found him alive. While he is still under the collapse.
that he was crushed. Smashed.
for the life of that hour. We desecrate the Sabbath even if he will live only a short time.
and found no breath in him. They discovered he is not breathing.
they checked and found the upper ones dead. They cleared the collapse and found that those in the upper part of the pile had died from the collapse.
rather, we clear for all. We clear everything necessary to find whoever was there.
we clear for all because of the Israelite. Perhaps he is there, and we are concerned that he is present because of his fixed residence in that courtyard.
one of them separated to another courtyard etc.. Even in this case the fixed presence of an Israelite in that courtyard is effective, to suspect that the trapped person is an Israelite.
for since all of them were uprooted, there is no fixed Israelite here. Unlike the previous halachah, where they were in fixed places.
on the presumption that he separated from the majority. In the case in question the majority are gentiles, so we do not clear.
if the majority were Israelites... we clear for him. For we follow the majority.
in the desert. An uninhabited place.
and does not know when the Sabbath day is. Who lost track of the count of days.
he counts from the day he erred six days and sanctifies the seventh. He begins counting six days from the day on which he lost count, and marks the seventh day as the Sabbath.

and he recites the blessing of the day over it and makes Havdalah at its close, as for the Sabbath. In this way he fulfils the positive commandment "Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy" (below 29:1), even though he does work on it.
he is permitted to do only enough for his livelihood. Only the work forbidden on the Sabbath that is needed to sustain his life.
and if he knows that today is the eighth day of his departure etc.. He has lost the general count of days, but knows how long he has been on the road.
and the other days apart from this day. Which may possibly be the Sabbath.
who besieged Israelite towns. Surrounded and laid siege.
we do not desecrate the Sabbath for them etc.. For this does not endanger lives.
that is near the border. An Israelite city close to the border of the Land.

matters of straw and chaff etc.. They wanted to plunder these things, which are not of great value. We fight them because the border must be guarded especially well, and the enemy must not be given a foothold there.
or if they besieged without specifying. Without it being known why they besieged, one must assume they intend war.
and when they have rescued their brethren etc.. After the rescue operation is over, they may return to their homes with their weapons.

so as not to cause them to stumble in the future. For if they could not return with their weapons, they might not come to rescue on the Sabbath in the future (see also below 27:17; for a similar law see Hilchot Shevitat Asor 3:6).
and likewise a ship tossed at sea or a city surrounded by a river. There is danger to life for those there.
or because he is pursued. An individual fleeing from someone pursuing him to kill him.
to repair weapons. To prepare weapons.
and we cry out for them and plead on the Sabbath. We pray that they be helped from heaven and saved.
and we sound the alarm for them to help them. We blow the shofar to summon people to gather and help (see also Hilchot Ta'aniyot 1:6, 2:3).

but we do not plead or cry out over a plague on the Sabbath. A pestilence among people. We do not pray about troubles on the Sabbath, because of the sanctity of the Sabbath (see ibid. 2:2, below 30:12).

three days before the Sabbath. And not less, so that the soldiers will settle their minds and not be alarmed and distracted on the Sabbath (below 30:13; compare Hilchot Melachim 6:11 and see Radbaz there).
an optional war. To expand the border of Israel and increase the greatness and fame of the king of Israel (ibid. 5:1).
from the tradition. The tradition of the Sages.

until it falls. "And you shall build siegeworks against the city that makes war with you, until it falls" - this refers to an optional war. Hence, a siege is to be maintained until the city is fully conquered.
in a commanded war. The war against the seven nations, the war against Amalek, and the aid of Israel from an enemy that came against them (Hilchot Melachim 6:1).

and Joshua conquered Jericho only on the Sabbath. For they encircled it for seven consecutive days (Joshua chapter 6), and according to the tradition of the Sages Jericho was conquered on the Sabbath.
is completed by itself. Continues and proceeds on its own, by virtue of the action done on Sabbath eve.
they open water channels. They open the water channel.
at dusk. Before nightfall and the onset of the Sabbath.
incense. Spices burned on coals.
under the garments. This incense is used to perfume clothes.
an eye bandage. A bandage for the eyes.
and a plaster. A bandage with ointment for wounds.
and they soak ink and dyes. In water, to prepare them as paint.
into the cauldron. A large pot containing dye (and see further below, halachah 17).
and bundles of flax into the oven. Bundles of threads, to be bleached in the oven.
and we load the beam of the olive press etc.. The grapes and olives, into the devices that press and squeeze them.
flowing. Liquids.
and they light... the bonfire from the eve. This should be done some time before night, so that it burns well when the Sabbath enters (see below, halachot 19-22).
they place a pot on the fire etc.. Before the Sabbath.
and eat them on the Sabbath. For even on the Sabbath itself one may enjoy work that was begun permissibly.
a decree, lest he stoke the coals on the Sabbath. He might stir the coals to kindle them and increase the heat, if he sees that the food needs it.
that has not cooked all it needs. That has not cooked completely.
and as long as it shrinks it improves for him. Leaving the food on the heat source, which causes it to shrink, improves its flavor.
a decree lest he stoke etc.. For the additional heat benefits these dishes.
swept the fire. Cleared the coals from the stove.
or the coals were dimmed. Even if he stokes them they will no longer ignite, and they are considered covered with ashes.
with gevavah. Straw and manure from the fields.
for he has put this dish out of his mind. Since he knows in advance that the fire beneath it is weak, he does not plan for the dish to cook further than it is now, but will eat it as it is.

on a stove whose steam is little. The top of the stove has room for two pots (below, halachah 7), and because of its width the heat in it is not high, and when there are no burning coals in it there is no possibility of additional cooking.
in an oven. Used for baking; because of the thickness of its walls and its shape, heat is retained in it better than in a stove.
and we do not lean it against it. We do not place it beside it so that it warms from its heat.
he does not put it out of his mind. From the possibility of cooking further.
even though it is swept. Though there are no coals at all in it to stoke.
most of the fire and its strength. The coals which produce most of the fire's power.
that not a single spark remain. Presumably some remnants of burning coals remained in the oven, which can be stoked.
the kuppach. A stove with room on top for one pot.
with olive pulp and with wood. Olive remains after the oil is pressed out, and pieces of wood that form coals, whose burning heat is great.
and it is permitted to lean against the stove. To place a dish beside the stove so that it warms from it; for the side of the stove is less hot than its top.
from the eve. But not on the Sabbath itself (below, halachah 10).
a raw dish that has not cooked at all. And it is placed on the fire close to the onset of the Sabbath to cook during the Sabbath.
that has cooked all it needs and shrinks and is harmed. Its prolonged stay on the heat source, which shrinks it, damages the dish.
a raw limb. A piece of meat not cooked at all.
close to twilight. A short time before the onset of the Sabbath (see below 5:4).

since he has already put it out of his mind. He is not occupied with that dish, since he cannot speed the cooking of raw meat by stoking the coals, but must wait for it to cook by itself. And a dish that shrinks and is harmed he will not stoke, since it damages that dish.
if he transgressed and left it. Intentionally.

and he shall wait until it could be made. At the end of the Sabbath one must wait a period of time sufficient to do the work; otherwise he would benefit from something forbidden having been done deliberately on the Sabbath, and might do so again (see also below 6:8).
and if he forgot it. He forgot the dish on the fire on Sabbath eve, and so left it there in a forbidden way.

if a dish that has not cooked all it needs etc.. The Sages penalized one who forgot in this matter, forbidding the dish on the Sabbath like the law of one who cooked on the Sabbath unintentionally, so that people will be careful about the Sages' ordinance to sweep the fire or cover it. There is no need to wait at the end of the Sabbath until it could be made (see below 6:23).

and if a dish that has cooked all it needs etc.. They penalized only where the forbidden leaving involves actual cooking; in this case there is no cooking, since it was already fully cooked from Sabbath eve (see below 9:3).
anything that is permitted to be left on the fire. On an open fire that is not swept and covered, such as food that is cooked and shrinks and is harmed (above, halachah 8).
it is forbidden to return it to its place. Even though the dish has already cooked fully.
provided he did not put the pot on the ground. For then it is evident that he is continuing the original leaving.
once he has put it down, we do not return it. For one who puts a pot on the stove appears to be cooking.
because their steam is very hot. And it is as if he is placing it on an open fire.
and anything onto which we do not return, we do not lean against it on the Sabbath. For leaning is also a way of cooking.
a fork. A large fork.
because he stirs with it, and this is part of the cooking. The fork is used for stirring, and stirring is an important act in the cooking process (see below 9:4; and also below, halachah 17).
and he is found to be cooking on the Sabbath. Even if he merely takes with a fork from a pot standing right on the fire and does not stir, he appears to be cooking.
to return from stove to stove. To move a pot to another stove.
whose steam is little. Its heat is lower.
for burying. For an insulating cover that retains heat. One may replace only with an insulation of the same kind, which is a continuation of the first (see also below 4:4).
lentils and lupines. Kinds of legumes.
even though they have not cooked at all. And one could have compared them to the case of a raw pot, which may be left even in an oven (above, halachah 8).
and his intention is to eat them right away. He does not put them out of his mind, and might stoke the coals.
and if he transgressed and left it etc.. As above, halachah 9.

an oven into which he put etc.. This halachah deals with leaving meat near a fire in order to roast it, and here there is no distinction between raw and not raw meat (unlike meat placed in a pot in the manner of cooking, whose laws were explained above, halachot 4-8, and unlike roast placed directly on coals, whose law will be explained below, halachah 16).
only the warmth of the fire. A low heat, and he will not come to stoke the coals.
and if the meat of a goat or ox. Which needs more heat to roast.
he plastered the mouth of the oven with clay. He sealed the oven with clay before the Sabbath, to preserve the oven's heat.
permitted. Even goat and ox meat.
the air will enter. The air from outside, and therefore there is no concern that he will come to stoke the coals.
it spoils. It ruins.
bundles of flax into the oven. Bundles of threads to be bleached in the oven (above, halachah 2).
he put in a whole kid. Not cut into limbs.
it is like goat meat etc.. It is not harmed by high heat.
unless he plastered the oven. As above, halachah 13.
the Paschal lamb. The Paschal offering, a kid or lamb roasted whole in the oven (see Hilchot Korban Pesach 8:10).
because the members of the group are zealous. They are meticulous about the commandment, and will not come to stoke the coals.
so that they will be roasted while it is still day and be fit to eat. So that there will be no need to hasten their cooking further.
because they are like something that shrinks and is harmed. Because of the damage caused to the dish if the coals are stoked.
and for this reason we place the incense under the garments at dusk. As explained above, halachah 2.
and it will smoke the garments. It will make the clothes stink with smoke instead of perfuming them.
it is not forbidden because it is done on the Sabbath. For the action began before the Sabbath (above, halachah 1).
wool into the cauldron. For dyeing in a large pot.
removed from the fire. Taken off the fire.
its mouth plastered with clay lest he stir. He seals the mouth of the cauldron so that he will not stir it on the Sabbath, for stirring is part of cooking (above, halachah 11).
a flat loaf. Flat dough, a pita.
so that a crust forms on the sides stuck to the oven or the fire. So that the side facing the heat hardens.
for if he stokes he will spoil them. He would damage the bread in the oven, and therefore they did not decree lest he stoke.
it is forbidden to eat from them etc.. Like the law of forbidden leaving (above, halachah 9).

he is permitted to scrape from it food for three Sabbath meals etc.. Scraping is forbidden as a rabbinic prohibition, but they permitted scraping with a change for the sake of Sabbath meals, and in a limited quantity (see also below 22:1).
a bonfire from anything he wishes. Any combustible material may be used, unlike the lighting of the Sabbath lamp, which has restrictions (see below 5:5-11).
and he uses its light etc.. There is no concern that he will tend the fire to increase light or heat (compare below 5:2, and there halachot 14-16).
a flame rising by itself. Burning as a flame, not as an ember.
a single log. One block of wood, which is the bonfire, with no other wood to ignite it.
most of its thickness. That the fire has penetrated its inner part.
and most of its circumference. That the fire has taken hold of most of the outer part of the wood.
in the provinces. Everywhere except the Temple.
at the bonfire of the Beit HaMoked. The place where the elder priests slept, where a fire was lit for warmth (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:9-11, 8:5).
for the priests are zealous. They are meticulous about the commandments, and there is no concern that they will stoke the coals.
a bonfire of reeds or of pits. Materials that burn easily.
if he bound the reeds. Tied them in a bundle.
in baskets. Woven baskets.
they are like wood. Their being gathered together delays the burning.
fat. Fat.
wax. Wax.
if he buried the dish in them. Covered the pot with them on all sides.
and manure. Animal dung used to fertilize the soil.
olive pulp. Olive remains after the oil is pressed out.
grape skins. Grape waste after pressing.
wool fluff. Clumps of wool.
moist by their own nature. They have not dried out of their natural moisture.
something that adds. Because they add to its cooking.
and clothing. Garments.
and dove feathers. Feathers.
and flax tow. Fragments that separate from the flax when it is combed.
carpenters. Woodworkers.
and hides. Skins.
and clippings of wool. Pieces of wool.

for we leave on a fire on the Sabbath. On an open fire, in cases where there is no concern of stoking the coals (above 3:8), since there is no prohibition of cooking regarding what was begun permissibly while it was still day (above 3:3).
and he will need to uncover it until the boiling subsides. To remove the material in which the pot is buried, in order to cool the heat of the dish somewhat.

and he will cover it again on the Sabbath. To restore the heat to the dish. This act is forbidden, as it is like returning to an open fire on the Sabbath (above 3:10), and he might do it by mistake because there is no fire here.
for ordinarily pots at twilight have already boiled and settled from their bubbling. They are brought to a boil on the fire while it is still day, and by twilight they have cooled a little.
and once they have settled they do not boil again. A second time, and therefore there is no need to decree lest he cover after it boils.
on the Sabbath itself. Such an act involves neither cooking nor even added heating.
lest he bury in embers. In coal ash, which has some heat and preserves the dish's heat.
and he will be found stoking the coals. In the course of burying, and kindling those sparks.
a doubt whether it is dark or not etc.. Twilight (for the definition of this time see below 5:4).

it is permitted to bury in something hot. They forbade burying in something that does not add heat only on the Sabbath for certain, and not at a time of doubt. And in something that adds heat it is permitted to bury at twilight, as there is no concern that the pot will boil (above, halachah 2).
until its chill passes. Until its coolness passes and it thaws.
and they were uncovered on the Sabbath. The covering material was removed from them.
for it does not add. The covering material does not add steam; but if he buried in something that adds steam (such as at twilight, see above, halachah 2), it is forbidden to return it (Yad Peshutah).

and it is permitted to replace the covering on the Sabbath etc.. Even though there is a difference in the level of heat retention of the various coverings, because this is a continuation of the first burying (see above 3:11).
he removed the dish or the water. Transferred them from the vessel in which they were originally cooked.
like something cold. Which may be buried even on the Sabbath itself (above, halachah 4).

for they forbade burying on the Sabbath only something hot that is in the first vessel in which it was cooked. But once it was transferred to a second vessel its heat has already diminished, and they did not decree against burying it.
a water heater. A water boiler.
and he plasters their mouth with dough. Seals the cover, to preserve the heat.
but so that they will stay warm from each other's heat. That they remain warm from each other's heat (Orah VeSimchah).
for it generates heat in it. Adds heat to it, and is similar to burying in something that adds heat.
and it is not like burying in something that adds. For this is not the act of burying that was forbidden by decree.
lighting a lamp for the Sabbath. Lighting it before the Sabbath, so that it will illuminate on Sabbath night.
is not optional etc.. The lighting is not optional, dependent on each person's wish whether to do it or not.

nor a commandment that he is not obligated to pursue etc.. There are commandments whose obligation arises following an act that is a matter of choice, and in this they resemble the optional (see Hilchot Berachot 11:2-3).

such as eruvei chatzerot. Which the Sages instituted to permit carrying on the Sabbath from a house to a courtyard (Hilchot Eruvin 1:2); if he does not want to carry, he is not obligated to make an eruv.
washing the hands for eating. The Sages instituted washing hands before eating bread (Hilchot Berachot 6:1-2); if he does not eat bread, he is not obligated to wash his hands.
but an obligation. That the Sages imposed on every person to do.
for this is part of the delight of the Sabbath. So that his house is not dark without a lamp.

just as he blesses over all the things he is obligated in by rabbinic enactment. Although the Torah has no explicit commandment about lighting lamps, the word "and has commanded us" refers to the commandment to obey the words of the Sages and keep all their ordinances (Hilchot Berachot 6:2, 11:3; and see Hilchot Mamrim 1:1-2).
to make use of the Sabbath lamp. To enjoy its light on Sabbath night (unlike the Hanukkah lamp, Hilchot Chanukah 4:6).
a decree lest he tilt. The lamp, to enlarge the light next to him (and see further below, halachot 14-16).
before sunset. For after sunset is a doubtful night, and no work is done then (below, halachah 4).
until three medium stars are seen. Then it is certainly considered night (see also Hilchot Terumot 7:2).
is the time called twilight everywhere. This time has significance for many laws in halachah.

and one who does work at twilight on Sabbath eve and at twilight at the end of the Sabbath etc.. If he did work both on Sabbath eve and at the end of the Sabbath at twilight, he certainly desecrated the Sabbath: if twilight counts as night, he desecrated the Sabbath at its entrance, and if it is day, he desecrated it before its exit.
from something that the flame does not hold well. From materials in which fire does not burn well.
and cedar fluff. Fibers found under the bark of the tree.
and flax that has not been beaten. Raw flax that has not been beaten into fibers.
and palm fiber. A woody material that grows around the palm in fibrous form.
fine linen. Linen fabric.
that he light most of the part of the wick that protrudes. That he ignite most of the part of the wick sticking out of the lamp, so that it burns well (see above 3:19).
something with which one may light. A wick of the materials from which it is permitted to light.
to thicken. To make it thick, because he wants the material that may not be used for lighting to burn as well.
standing. Upright.

we put a grain of salt... so that it burns on Sabbath nights. It is permitted to place a grain at the place where the wick emerges from the vessel, to limit the size of the flame and slow the burning of the lamp. And we do not worry that he might forget and remove it on the Sabbath to increase the light (Yad Peshutah).
we make a bonfire of them. It is permitted to use them for a bonfire, as there are no restrictions on burning materials in it (above 3:19).
on a lampstand. Even though this resembles a lamp.
draws after the wick. Is drawn up and burns well through it.
and tail fat and fat. Animal fat.
lest the light of the lamp be dim. That it will not shine properly.
and he will tilt it. The lamp, to enlarge the flame, and so he will be kindling a fire on the Sabbath.
that he melted. Heated until it melted.
that dissolved. Were mashed until they became like oil.

he puts into them any amount of oil. He mixes into them a little oil that is permitted for lighting. For these oils that have dissolved are absorbed by the wick and burn well only in liquid state, not if they congeal and freeze. In a mixture with kosher oil they stay liquid and are drawn properly after the wick (R. Y. Kafih).
but oils with which one does not light... that are not drawn. Therefore there is no benefit in mixing into them oil that is permitted for lighting.
in itran. An oily liquid that is a by-product of producing tar.
and he is obligated to sit by the light of the lamp. This is part of the delight of the Sabbath (above, halachah 1).
with balsam. A fragrant resin from perfume trees.
lest he take from it from the lamp. To use the perfume (and see below, halachah 12).
volatile. Evaporates and is flammable.
in white naphtha. Refined.
on a weekday. On an ordinary day.
and he will come to danger. Of a fire.
in other oils. All other oils not mentioned as forbidden.
so that it drips. Drops of oil into the lamp slowly.
the head of the wick. The end of the wick.
lest he take from the oil in the vessel. From that oil intended to burn on the Sabbath, which is forbidden as extinguishing since it hastens the extinguishing of the lamp (below 12:2).
for it has not been rendered repulsive by the lamp. For it is in a separate vessel, and is not dirty and repulsive for use like the oil in the lamp itself.
and it is forbidden to benefit on the Sabbath from the oil in which it was lit etc.. Even where it is not extinguishing, if one takes from the oil.
muktzeh because of a prohibition. For it was forbidden to use at the onset of the Sabbath because of the prohibition of extinguishing (see below 26:14).
and if he attached the vessel... it is permitted. To light with it, for in such a case there is no concern that he will use the oil, since it is evident that it is meant for the burning lamp.
to receive oil in it. Dripping from the lamp.

he disqualifies the vessel from its preparation. He causes the vessel to become forbidden to move on the Sabbath. The vessel was permitted for use before, and when muktzeh oil drips into it on the Sabbath, it becomes forbidden to move (below 25:23).
and if he placed it while it was still day, it is permitted. For he did not disqualify it from its preparation on the Sabbath.
sparks. Burning fragments falling from the lamp.
because they have no substance. They burn out immediately and do not remain in the vessel.
and it is forbidden to put water into it. Into the vessel placed under the lamp to receive the sparks.
because he brings the extinguishing of the sparks closer. For they are extinguished immediately upon falling into the water, and this is like an act of extinguishing.
we do not search for lice by lamplight. It is forbidden to examine clothes for lice by lamplight, for it is a thing requiring careful inspection (above, halachah 2).
and even if it is high etc.. Even if the lamp is in a place he certainly cannot touch.
and he will tilt. The lamp, to improve its light (as above, halachah 9).
for each of them is occupied with his own matter. And he is not likely to notice that his fellow forgets and tilts the lamp.
the children. Boys.
for the teacher watches them. That they do not tilt, like two who read the same matter, where each reminds the other (above, halachah 14).
whose fear is not upon him. And they will not remind him because they are afraid of him.
and he may look in the book etc.. He is permitted to find the beginning of the passage, for this is not reading requiring study but merely a glance.
and to distinguish between them. To tell the vessels apart.
a non-regular attendant. A servant not accustomed to those vessels.
whether by a naphtha lamp whose light is great. And nevertheless it is forbidden, lest he tilt.

we do not instruct him to examine etc.. Although there is no concern that a regular attendant will tilt, we do not teach him that it is permitted to examine by the light of an olive oil lamp, lest it lead to another mishap - that he take from the oil, and so be found extinguishing.
a lamp behind the door. The lamp is placed near the door or fixed to it on its inner side.
because he extinguishes it. If he opens the door or closes it quickly in his usual manner, the lamp goes out because of it.
so that the wind blows on it. Intending to fan the bonfire.
even though there is only a common wind. An ordinary wind, and fanning with such wind is not certain.

and we place the Sabbath lamp on a tree attached to the ground and he need not worry. There is no concern that he will come to use the tree, since moving the lamp is forbidden on the Sabbath (for the prohibition of using something attached to the ground see below 21:6). But on a festival, when it is permitted to move the lamp, it is forbidden to place it on the tree (Hilchot Yom Tov 4:5).
six blasts on Sabbath eve. Three blasts to mark the times to cease from work, and three to separate holy from profane (detailed below, halachah 19; and see Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 7:6).
its outskirts. The fields and areas around the city that belong to it (see below 27:1).

and those who are near may not enter the city until those who are far arrive and they all enter at once. So that it is evident that they enter the city in honor of the Sabbath. Some explain: so that those far away will not be suspected of having continued working after the blast (Me'iri citing Rashi).
and the shutters are in place. The doors of the shops on which the merchandise sold in the shops is placed.
the remover removed. Took the pots off the stove.
and the burier buried. The pots in heat-retaining materials.

and he waits long enough to roast etc.. After the third blast he waits a short time, the time needed for the last preparations before the Sabbath, and then blows the three blasts that separate profane from holy.
at Minchah. Toward evening, about two and a half hours before sunset (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesachim 10:1).
to permit the people to their work. To announce that the Sabbath has ended and all work is permitted.

they did not blow. On Yom Kippur to announce the entrance of the Sabbath, since the blast is meant to announce the beginning of the Sabbath prohibitions, and these already apply on Yom Kippur itself, as the work prohibitions of Yom Kippur and of the Sabbath are equal (Hilchot Shevitat Asor 1:2). All this applies when they sanctified the month by sighting; but nowadays the Sabbath and Yom Kippur are not adjacent (see Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh 7:1, 7:7 and Piskei VeShitot there).

we neither blow nor make Havdalah. We do not blow to announce that the Sabbath has ended, nor do we make Havdalah in the prayer or over a cup, because the work prohibitions of the Sabbath continue into Yom Kippur.

we blow but do not make Havdalah. We blow to announce the beginning of the work prohibitions of the Sabbath, which are stricter than those of a festival (see Hilchot Yom Tov 1:4). We do not make Havdalah, since it is a transition from lesser sanctity to greater sanctity (see below 29:18).

we make Havdalah but do not blow. We make Havdalah from greater sanctity to lesser sanctity ("who distinguishes between holy and holy," below 29:22), and do not blow to announce the end of the Sabbath prohibitions, because blowing on a festival is forbidden by a rabbinic prohibition (see Hilchot Shofar 2:6-7), and it is not set aside to announce a permission.
to do work for us on the Sabbath. For the Israelite's needs.
for he is not commanded concerning the Sabbath. For the Sabbath is a sign between the Holy One and Israel (below 30:15), and was not given to gentiles (see Hilchot Melachim 10:9).

the Sabbath light in their eyes. If the Sabbath is desecrated by gentiles for the sake of Israelites, it would be disrespect for the sanctity of the Sabbath, and Israelites might come to desecrate the Sabbath themselves.
on his own. Without having been asked by an Israelite.

and he shall wait long enough for it to be made. At the end of the Sabbath one must wait a period of time sufficient to do the work, so that the Israelite will have no benefit from the work having been done for him on the Sabbath (see below, halachah 8).
that the matter not be public. With great publicity; see below, halachot 5-6, 12.
for himself. For the gentile's own purpose.
a gentile who lit the lamp. For himself.
lest he do more in his work for him. For if the gentile knows him, he might draw more water and pick more grass than he needs, so that the Israelite can use it afterward.
for there is no more or less in it. The same action is done whether for one use or for many users.
at a banquet. A place where many people recline together.
for one who lights lights according to the majority. The lamp was lit for the diners, and therefore we follow the majority.
half and half is forbidden. Even if there is no majority of Israelites but exactly half, it is considered as if he lit also for them.

we do not say to him extinguish or do not extinguish. We do not ask him to extinguish, but we also do not prevent him from extinguishing even though it is for the Israelite's benefit; rather he does as he wishes.
because his rest is not our responsibility. Israelites are not commanded to prevent the gentile from desecrating the Sabbath if he wants to (see below, halachah 21; and see also below 12:7).
a dead person for whom gentiles made etc.. An Israelite died, and gentiles took trouble for his burial and did work on the Sabbath.
he shall wait long enough for them to be made. So that there will be no benefit from the desecration of the Sabbath (above, halachah 2).
on a main road. A highway.
and all passers-by and captives say etc.. That the desecration of the Sabbath for that dead person became publicly known.
and it is permitted to bury another Israelite in it. For the prohibition is only because of the disgrace to the person for whom these things were done.
even though they brought them from the side of the wall. Although it is known that he brought them only a short distance until bringing them into the city (Orah VeSimchah).
he shall wait... long enough for them to come from a nearby place. They wait the time it takes to bring the flutes from the nearest settlement where they might have been.
perhaps they brought them at night etc.. And because of this concern, this period of waiting must be added.
from such-and-such a place. From a particular, known place.
as we said. Above, halachah 5.
a bathhouse that heats on the Sabbath. A bathhouse operated on the Sabbath, where water is heated for the bathers.
if the majority are gentiles, it is permitted to bathe in it right at the end of the Sabbath. For the water is heated for all the bathers, and we follow the majority (above, halachah 4).
and if the majority are Israelites, he shall wait long enough for water to heat. That is, long enough for the work to be done (above, halachah 2).
and we give him lashes for rebelliousness. Lashes by rabbinic decree.

and they did not forbid it everywhere... except for this reason. The reason that in every work done by a gentile for an Israelite they required waiting long enough for it to be done is the reason that will be explained.
for if you say it is permitted immediately. If it were permitted to use right at the end of the Sabbath.
lest he tell the gentile to do it for him and find the matter ready immediately. At the end of the Sabbath, so that in any case he benefits from having told the gentile to desecrate the Sabbath.
he does not profit. He does not gain.

something that is not work and is forbidden to do on the Sabbath only as a shevut. Things forbidden by the Sages as a safeguard against work (above 1:3), and likewise things that resemble work or that have a decree lest he come to a stoning-level prohibition (below 21:1).

provided there is some illness there etc.. These are special considerations because of which the prohibition of telling a gentile is set aside for prohibitions that are only shevut (and see below 24:10 regarding twilight).
to climb a tree or to swim on the surface of the water. Which are forbidden as shevut (below 21:6, 23:5).
in order to bring him a shofar. On Rosh Hashanah, which is a festival, and these shevut prohibitions apply on it (Hilchot Yom Tov 1:17).

or a knife for circumcision. Although the performance of the commandment of circumcision overrides the Sabbath (Hilchot Milah 2:6), bringing the articles for the commandment does not. But in a shevut prohibition they permitted it through a gentile (see also ibid. 2:9).
from courtyard to courtyard between which there is no eruv. For carrying between them is forbidden by rabbinic law (Hilchot Eruvin 1:1-2).
one who buys a house in the Land of Israel. Bought from a gentile; this involves the commandment of settling the Land of Israel.
forbidden by their words. As above, halachah 1.

and because of settling the Land of Israel they did not decree in this matter. They did not forbid telling a gentile even in the case of the prohibition of writing, which is from the Torah (below 11:9), because of the merit of this commandment.
in Syria. The territories conquered by King David north of the Land of Israel, which have the status of the Land of Israel for some laws (see Hilchot Terumot 1:3-4).
he contracts... and fixes the payment. He sets the scope of the work and the fixed pay for it.

and the gentile does it for himself, and even though he works on the Sabbath it is permitted. For he was not hired for work on the Sabbath specifically but as a contractor, and if he wants to work on the Sabbath to finish faster, he is working for himself.
one who hires a gentile for many days... he works whenever he wishes. For he too was not hired to work specifically on the Sabbath, and if he wants to work on the Sabbath he does so for himself.
provided he does not reckon with him day by day. Provided he does not calculate the wage of each day separately, for then it turns out he hired him to work on the Sabbath.
if it was known, evident and publicized. That the work is that of an Israelite.
that he fixed. That he fixed a set payment for that work as a contract.
to build his courtyard etc.. For usually it is known to whom these things belong.
in the town or within the boundary. In the city or in the area near it that can be reached from the city on the Sabbath.
to lease his vineyard or field to a gentile. That the gentile will work them, and pay the Israelite a fixed rent or a share of the produce of the field.
for one who sees knows that they are hired, or that he went down to them as a sharecropper. For so it is customary with fields and vineyards.
for the Israelite's name is called upon it as its owner. For it is publicly known as belonging to a particular Israelite.

because we are not commanded about the rest of vessels etc.. That no forbidden work be done with them; unlike an animal and a slave, whose rest we were commanded (see below chapter 20, halachot 1-3, 14).
if they stipulated at the outset etc.. That this condition was in the partnership agreement from the beginning (compare Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 10:14).

if they stipulated at the outset that the Sabbath earnings go to the gentile etc.. That whatever they earn on the Sabbath days will go to the gentile, and the profits of one of the weekdays will go to the Israelite, so that they are not partners at all in the Sabbath work.
the gentile takes all the Sabbath earnings by himself. The Israelite may not share in it, for he would be a partner in the gentile's work.
and the Sabbath earnings were not known. No calculation was made of exactly how much the forbidden profits are.
the Sabbatical year. Shemittah.
one who gives money to a gentile to deal with. To trade with, and they share the profits.

shares the profit with him equally, and so all the Geonim ruled. For the gentile alone deals with it as he wishes, and this is unlike a shop in partnership in which both work together (responsum of Rav Sherira Gaon, cited in Beit Yosef, sec. 245).
vessels for a gentile craftsman to make. Items for repair.
that he contracted with him. He fixed the price, so the gentile is considered to be doing the work for himself (above, halachah 12).
enough time for him to leave his house before dark. So that he can leave the Israelite's house with the vessels before the Sabbath begins.
he shall give him a pledge. He shall give him a security. [Note: Rambam in his Commentary on the Mishnah vocalizes the word aimati: ammatai.]
a letter. A letter.
if he fixed with him the fee for carrying. He set the price of the delivery in advance (as above, halachah 12).
provided he left with it from the door of his house etc.. As above, halachah 19.

if there is a fixed person in the town who collects the letters etc.. If in that city there is a central post office to which letters come, and the gentile takes the letter to the post office and not all the way to its destination.

provided there is enough daylight for him to reach the house next to the wall etc.. So that he could reach the edge of the city before the Sabbath begins, since the post office may be in a distant place. And there is no problem that the postal courier carries the letter on the Sabbath, since he is not the agent of the Israelite himself but of the post office.
a gentile who brought his goods on the Sabbath and brought them into an Israelite's house. To deposit them there.
permitted. Even on the Sabbath itself, since there is no concern of appearances (as above, halachah 19) regarding the gentile's own goods.
and even if he said to him, put them in this corner. In which the Israelite helps that gentile slightly with his work and shows that he is content with it.
this is permitted. For the gentile brought them in on his own initiative.
and we invite the gentile on the Sabbath. It is permitted to invite him to eat with an Israelite (but on a festival it is forbidden to invite him, see Hilchot Yom Tov 1:13).
we do not attend to him. We do not interfere with his actions.
we place food before the dog in the courtyard. If the responsibility for its food rests on that person (see below 29:36).
and the day became holy upon him. The Sabbath began while he was on his way.
and he had money with him. And it is forbidden to carry it four cubits in the public domain.

he gives his purse to a gentile etc.. He gives his wallet to a gentile. This is permitted, although the gentile is doing work for the Israelite on the Sabbath, and even without the conditions mentioned above for permission: fixing a wage (above, halachah 12) and transferring the object before the Sabbath (above, halachah 19).
anxious. Worried and apprehensive.
and if you do not permit this etc.. If telling a gentile were forbidden even in this case, he might transgress a Torah prohibition (and see further below 20:6-7).
a found object. That he found on the road, and wants to carry to his house.

he may not give it to the gentile. For the reason "a person is anxious about his money" does not apply to a found object, since he did not toil for it, and so here they did not permit telling a gentile.
he carries it in less than four cubits at a time. For one is not liable for carrying when he goes each time less than four cubits and stops (as below 13:10).
it is forbidden for him to benefit from that work forever. The Sages penalized him for the transgression he committed, so that he cannot benefit from its products.
at the end of the Sabbath right away. Without waiting "long enough for it to be made" (compare above, halachah 8). But on the Sabbath itself it is forbidden because of the carrying done in it.
and its products are not holy. The products of the work done on it are not forbidden as sacred, namely as things consecrated to the Temple that are forbidden for all use.
and if he cooked unintentionally at the end of the Sabbath, he may eat... right away. For they did not penalize the unintentional offender by forbidding it to him after the Sabbath.
that went outside the boundary and returned. They were taken out beyond two thousand cubits, which is the limit one may walk on the Sabbath (below 27:1), and were brought back to their place.
for no act was done to their bodies and they did not change. And therefore they are not forbidden because of the carrying done with them.
if deliberately, they may not be eaten until the end of the Sabbath. For the Sages penalized the deliberate offender in this case.
he shall not give him his Sabbath wage. For it is forbidden to receive payment for work on the Sabbath.
he has no responsibility on the Sabbath. He is not considered a hired guard on Sabbaths, and if the things are damaged at that time he does not pay.
a Sabbath worker. For a whole week.
he gives him his full wage. He pays for the whole period, Sabbaths included, and in this way the Sabbath wage is not distinguishable.

and he shall not say to him, give me my Sabbath wage. Do not make a distinction between the Sabbath wage and the wage for the rest of the time, since he would then be considered as receiving payment for work on the Sabbath.
some are principal categories and some are derivatives. Divided into branches of principal categories and their derivatives, as will be explained in this chapter.
and the number of all principal categories of work is thirty-nine etc.. The definitions and laws of the various types of work will be detailed in the following chapters.
and gathering sheaves. Gathering grain into a heap.
and threshing. The labor of separating the kernels from their husks.
and winnowing. Tossing the grain in the wind after threshing so that the chaff separates from the kernels.
and sifting. Sifting the flour.
and shearing. Shearing wool.
and bleaching. Cleaning the wool.
and beating. Separating the fibers and preparing them for spinning.
and making the loops. Threading the warp threads into the weaving apparatus.
and stretching the warp. Stretching the warp threads.
and unraveling. Pulling threads out of the fabric.
and tanning. Processing the hide.
and scraping the hide. Smoothing it.
and ruling lines. Marking lines on the parchment for writing.
and anything of their kind. Works that are identical in their action or are done for the same purpose.
this is a principal category of work. All of them fall under the principal category "plowing," and are not derivatives (and see below 8:1).
one who layers trees. Plants in the ground a shoot still attached to a tree in order to grow a new tree from it.
one who grafts. Attaches a cutting or branch to the stock (trunk) of an already planted tree.
one who prunes. Cuts the branches of a tree to improve it.
one who harvests grain etc.. All these labors are essentially the same labor, applied to different kinds of produce.
a derivative is a labor that resembles a principal category. It has an aspect of similarity to the principal labor, but not identity of substance.
little by little. In small pieces (see below 21:18).
a piece. A piece.
and rubbed. Scrapes and crumbles it (below 8:15).
and put rennet in it. Placed in the milk a small piece of stomach lining, which contains substances that cause cheese to curdle (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 3:13).
separated the curd from the milk. Caused the whey to separate from the congealing substance (see also below 8:11).
and if he shaped it into a cheese. To make it a single solid mass.
it resembles building. And it becomes a derivative of building (see below 10:13).
and from the nature of the work done on the Sabbath etc.. By examining the purpose or form of the work, one can know to which category it belongs.
if deliberately, he is liable to karet etc.. For there is no difference between principal categories and derivatives in the severity of their prohibition on the Sabbath.
a fixed sin offering. See above 1:1.

in one lapse of awareness. In a single lapse, without his having become aware between one work and another that those works are forbidden on the Sabbath. One who commits the same transgression several times in one lapse of awareness brings one sin offering. If he became aware between them, that awareness divides it into two sin offerings (Hilchot Shegagot 5:1).
if he did many principal categories... he is liable for one sin offering for each principal category. For each labor is considered a separate transgression (ibid. 7:3).
and if he did a principal category and its derivatives... he is liable for only one sin offering. Likewise if he did several derivatives of the same principal category (ibid. 7:5).
he did the thirty-nine unintentionally. That he did all the principal categories of labor.

many works of the same kind of one work... he is liable for only one sin offering. Even in this case he is liable for only one, although they are not a principal category and its derivatives (see also Hilchot Shegagot 7:7).
one who plows any amount. Even the smallest amount, for it is fit for sowing.
one who weeds around the roots of trees. Digs around the roots of trees to clear the soil.
and one who trims. Cuts.
one who prunes the shoots. Cuts thin branches.
one who levels the surface of the field. Evens out the area.
who lowered the mound and flattened it. Lowered the raised place and leveled it.
filled the ravine. Added earth in the low place.
anyone who levels pits. Evens the surface (for the rabbinic prohibitions of plowing see below 21:2-4).
one who prunes a tree so that it will grow. Cuts the branches to improve its growth or the growth of its fruit.
of the kind of sowing. Of the kind of the principal category itself, and not defined as a derivative (see above 7:3).
one who waters... this is a derivative of sowing. Because it aids growth, and in this it resembles sowing.
one who soaks wheat and barley and the like in water. To make them sprout, and this act resembles sowing (for the rabbinic prohibitions of sowing see below 21:5).
the size of a dried fig. The size of a fig, which is an important measure in labors connected with food production.
and one who uproots. Pulls something growing out of the ground (for the rabbinic prohibitions of harvesting see below 21:6-10).
one who uproots something from its growing place. Who detaches it and removes it from the medium in which it grew, even if it was not actually attached to the ground.
a clod. A clump of earth.
and dodder that climbed on a thornbush. Dodder is a parasitic plant that draws nourishment from another plant (a thornbush).
and grasses that grew on the back of a barrel. Because of the barrel's moisture, a kind of mold or green growth grew on its surface.
from an unperforated pot. A vessel with no hole in its bottom; a plant in it is considered detached from the ground for many halachic purposes.
he is exempt, because this is not its growing place. For this plant ordinarily grows attached to the ground.
a pot perforated to the size of a small root. A hole of this size makes it considered attached to the ground (see Hilchot Terumot 5:15 and elsewhere).
whose harvesting makes it grow and enlarge. For the cutting benefits its growth.
alfalfa. Alfalfa (generally used as fodder for horses).
and beet greens. Beet leaves.
and one because he plants. For this falls under the labor of sowing (above 7:3).
and he needs the wood. He wants to use it.
and placed it on pegs. While it hangs in the air.
he is liable for uprooting. For he detached the plants from their nourishment in the ground.
figs that dried on their stems. Dried while still attached to the branches of the tree.

even though they are like detached with regard to impurity. Although they become impure with food impurity as if they were detached (Hilchot Tum'at Ochalin 2:5), with regard to the Sabbath they are considered attached.
endive. The endive plant, whose leaves are used as food.
and one who trims shoots. Cuts soft branches fit for eating; since this act suits various purposes, the measure for the labor is determined by the purpose the person intended.
if for eating. That a person will eat them.
and if for fuel. To light a fire with them.
enough to cook an egg. For the definition of this measure see the next paragraph.
one who gathers foods. Collects them together.
and the egg mentioned everywhere. The measure "the size of an egg" mentioned often in halachah.
a medium egg. Of medium size.
enough to cook a dried fig's worth of an egg etc.. The heat required to cook a dried fig's measure of that egg.

and gathering applies only to products of the ground. The prohibition of gathering applies only to things that are plant species (for the rabbinic prohibitions of gathering see below 21:11). [Note: In his Commentary on the Mishnah, Rambam vocalizes the word "chickens" as tarnogelin.]
one who gathers a fig cake and made a round out of it. Pressed and packed figs together into a round vessel.
that they gathered into one body. Joined together.
one who threshes. Separates the grains of wheat from the husk surrounding them by applying strong pressure to the ears.
and threshing applies only to products of the ground. The principal category "threshing" applies only to products of the ground.

and one who extracts. An act of separation, such as extracting liquid from a solid. This act is a derivative of threshing because there is a similarity between them (see above 7:5), and it applies also to things that are not products of the ground (for the rabbinic prohibitions of extracting see below 21:12-16).
one who milks... because he extracts. For he separates the milk from the animal (see also below, halachah 10).
one who wounds a living creature that has skin. Struck it so that blood came out (see also below, halachah 9).
provided he needs the blood etc.. For feeding a dog and the like.
he is exempt because he is destroying. For so is the law of one who destroys without need (above 1:17).
one who wounds an animal or beast. In which wounding is destruction, unless he intends to use the blood.
one who wounds his fellow. Struck and injured another person.
his mind cooled and his anger subsided. He calmed down from his anger.
and he is like one who repairs. And not one who destroys (for this principle see below 10:10).

the eight creeping creatures mentioned in the Torah. Which the Torah distinguished from other vermin and creepers, and which impart impurity at their death (Leviticus 11:29-30; for their laws see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ah chapter 4).
they have no skin, therefore one who wounds them is exempt. Since they have no skin, extracting blood from them is not considered an act of extracting.
where the blood gathered. Collected under the skin at the place of the wound.
one who squeezes fruits is liable for extracting. For it is an act of producing liquid from a solid body.
and one is liable from the Torah only for pressing olives and grapes. For it is their way to be squeezed, since oil and wine have importance in themselves.
for a liquid that comes for food is food. Since the liquid mixes directly with the food, it has no status of a liquid at all.
and he is found to be separating food from food. And there is no act of extracting here.
he is a presser. Considered as if pressing them in the usual way.

one who milks into food, or one who suckles with his mouth, is exempt. For this is not the way of milking (Orah VeSimchah). And it is not permitted on the ground that it separates food from food, since the animal is not considered food (for the permission to suckle with the mouth see below 21:14).
one who winnows. Tosses the grain toward the wind so that it carries off the chaff and cleans the grain of it.
one who selects. Separates between parts of a mixture.
and one who churns. Shakes milk to gather its fatty parts into butter.
one who strains. Removes and cleans.
one who sifts. Sifts flour (for their rabbinic prohibitions see below 21:17, 21:32).

this is a derivative of selecting or a derivative of sifting... their matters resemble each other. The Sages disagreed about which of the principal categories to assign the labor of straining out dregs, since the basic purpose of these principal categories is the same: cleaning the food from the waste mixed in it.
and why did they count them as three. As three different principal categories, with liability for a sin offering for each separately.

for every labor that was in the Tabernacle is counted by itself. All the acts done there are considered labors in their own right, since the Torah used the term "melachah" for the work of the Tabernacle, as in the Sabbath prohibitions (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 7:2).
one who selects food from waste. Cleaned the food by taking it out from the husks and dirt.
two kinds of foods. Mixed together, and he wants to separate them.
with a sieve or a screen. Kinds of strainers, that is, vessels designated for the labor of selecting.
with a tray or a bowl. A platter and a dish, in which large quantities can be sorted but which are not vessels specifically for sorting.
by hand. Without a utensil.
to eat right away. To eat in the near future.
and one who selects waste from food, even by hand, is liable. For this is the actual way of selecting.

and one who selects lupines etc.. The lupine is a legume with bitterness; to make it fit to eat it is boiled with its husk ("their waste"), which absorbs the lupine's bitterness. The commentators found this halachah difficult, and perhaps it can be said that it speaks of the stage before cooking, removing some of the lupines from the mixture and leaving their husks, in order to reduce the proportion of the fruit so that the dish will not end up too bitter. Therefore, one who removes the bitter lupines is considered as selecting waste from food, since by removing the lupines he improves the rest of the mixture (Yad Peshutah explains similarly; see there).
to leave it. To leave it sorted, and not to eat it right away.
even for use later in the day. Even if he intends to use it later that day.
like one who sorts for storage. For storing, which is certainly a labor.
and leaves it to eat immediately. He leaves the separated kinds in order to eat one of them soon.
one who strains... with their strainer. Filters with a special vessel designed to catch the dregs and let clear liquid through.

but one may strain wine that has no dregs, or clear water, through cloths and an Egyptian basket. A cloth or basket, which are not the regular strainer. In this way one may filter only a drink that is already clear, in which case the additional straining is not considered a labor.

and we put water on the dregs so that it will become clear. Adding water to wine dregs in the vessel, so that the wine absorbed in them is separated (R. Y. Kafih). This is not like selecting, because the wine mixed with the dregs is itself considered dregs, and they are like one body from which he separated its part, as explained further in the halachah (Orah VeSimchah).

and we put a beaten egg into a mustard strainer so that it will clear. Putting it into the mustard creates a separation between the coarse and fine parts of the mustard (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 20:2). Here too the reason is that all the mustard is like one body (see also Hilchot Yom Tov 3:17, that it is forbidden to strain directly through a strainer because it looks like selecting).
and mustard that he kneaded on Sabbath eve. He mixed it with water and prepared it for eating.
strains it. Removes the inferior part from the mixture (see also below 22:12).
beats. Mixes.
for the dregs have not yet separated... and all the wine is like one body. Everything is still considered one substance, and so one can say there is no separation here between food and waste.
and likewise the mustard. It too is all considered one body, and so there is no separation of food from waste.
one who grinds. Crushes and pulverizes.
and one who chops detached vegetables. Into small pieces to cook them (see above 7:5; for the rabbinic prohibitions of grinding see below 21:18-31).
to benefit from their sawdust. To use the sawdust specifically. But if he intends to use the wood he cut, he is liable for cutting (below 11:7).
one who files a tongue of metal. Filed and pulverized a piece of metal.
but one who chops wood etc.. For wood waste is presumably meant for fuel (see above, halachah 5).
and one who sifts. Sifts flour.
and one who kneads earth. Mixes it with water to make mortar (for the rabbinic prohibitions of kneading see below 21:33-36).
enough to make the opening of a goldsmiths' furnace. The measure needed to seal the small opening of a furnace in which gold is refined.

and there is no kneading with ashes etc.. Mixing these materials with water is not considered kneading, since they do not become a sticky dough (see Hilchot Yom Tov 3:10; and see further below 21:33-34).
they mix and cling to one another. They stick together even if he did not knead.
the spices. Dyestuffs or substances used for medicine and the like.
it is all of one kind. They are identical labors done for the same purpose (see above 7:2). For the rabbinic prohibitions of cooking see below 22:1-12.
a small limb. The little toe of a one-day-old infant (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 8:1).

so that they are fit for the purpose for which they are cooked. For example, if cooking for dyeing, its measure is as below in halachah 14; and if for other needs (such as medicine), according to what is fitting for that need (Yad Peshutah).
so that it will be rolled. So that it cooks from the heat of the urn until it hardens a little.
for one who cooks with derivatives of fire. By something heated by fire (in this case, the urn).
one who rinses in hot water. Pours hot water over.
old salted fish. Fish that was salted long ago.
one who breaks. Breaks (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 3:2).
that was roasted. Was entirely cooked by its heat.
for derivatives of the sun. Objects heated by the sun.

they decreed concerning them because of derivatives of fire. That it is forbidden to cook with them initially, because of the similarity to derivatives of fire (but in the sun itself it is permitted to cook, as below 22:9).
in the hot springs of Tiberias. Hot spring water. [Note: Rambam vocalizes this word: Tevarya.]
exempt. Since they are not heated by the heat of fire, and their law is like derivatives of the sun.
one who cooks... something that was already cooked... is exempt. For this act is not defined as cooking (and see further below 22:8).

one put in the fire and one put in the wood... all are liable for cooking. For each of these acts is significant when done, and they are part of the cooking process (Yad Peshutah, and see Piskei VeShitot).
and stirred. Stirred the dish.
for anyone who does something that is a need of cooking is a cook. Even if he does not actually cook, because he contributed to the cooking.
but if one placed the pot. Set the pot on the stove.

only the last two are liable for cooking. From the standpoint of the labor of cooking, the acts done at first were useless, and only kindling a large fire after the wood was brought is the beginning of the cooking.
if a dried fig's worth was roasted in it, even in two or three places. If the roasted parts are combined, they total the measure of a dried fig.
on one side. Only the side facing the coals was cooked, and he did not turn the meat so that the other side would cook too.
he is permitted to scrape it before it is baked and it comes to labor. Although scraping is forbidden as shevut (below 12:1), they permitted scraping where it prevents a transgression.
one who melts. Heats the metal until it becomes liquid.
until it becomes a coal. Until it glows and softens until it is workable.
one who dissolves. Melts.
and kofer. A kind of tar (perhaps referring to the substance called camphor in foreign languages, used for perfume and healing), whose crystals are dissolved to make oil from it.
one who bakes earthenware vessels until they become potsherds. Fires them in a kiln.
the hide. A flayed skin.

and it is about two thirds of a span. A span is half a cubit, that is, three handbreadths, so that the width of a sit is about two handbreadths. A double sit is therefore four handbreadths (and see below, halachah 10).
one who plucks a wing feather. A feather.
and one who spins wool from a living animal. While attached and without having sheared it.
for this is not the way of shearing etc.. For this is not the usual way of the labor.
this is a derivative of shearing. For in these too he removes parts attached to the body of a living creature. For the rabbinic prohibitions of shearing see below 22:13-14.
and provided he takes with a utensil. For that is the way of cutting them.
a wart. A callus.
whether by hand or by utensil, he is exempt. For this is not shearing of something that grows in the ordinary way, but it is forbidden as repairing the skin.

and it is permitted to cut a callus in the Temple by hand. A callus is a blemish that disqualifies a priest from serving in the Temple and an animal from being offered (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 7:8); therefore they permitted cutting the callus here in order to qualify the priest, and did not decree this shevut where it would delay the Temple service (for this principle see also below 10:6, 21:27, 22:25, Hilchot Korban Pesach 8:18).
but not with a utensil. For although they permitted shevut in the Temple, it is still preferable to depart from the usual way.
and if it was dry, he may cut it even with a utensil. Here the repair is lesser because the callus crumbles by itself.
he picked white ones from among black ones etc.. For the removal of each is significant.
a nail that is mostly detached. Mostly separated from the body.
and strips of skin. Thin strips of skin.
upward. That were torn toward the body, and may injure it more if they remain.
it is permitted to take them by hand. For he does not intend to repair but to prevent pain.
and if the majority has not separated. They are considered attached to his body and it is forbidden to cut them as a derivative of shearing.
one who bleaches. Cleans.
silk. Silk.
and one who launders garments is a derivative of bleaching. For they are labors whose purpose is cleaning cloth. For the rabbinic prohibitions of laundering see below 22:15-22.
for wringing is part of laundering. A stage in the labor of laundering.
just as stirring is part of cooking. See above 3:11.
and there is no wringing of hair. Because it does not absorb the water.
one who beats wool. Beats the fibers or combs them in order to separate them from one another.
and one who beats sinews. Pounds animal sinews until they soften.
a lasting dye. That remains for a long time.
sarak or shashar. Kinds of dyes. For the rabbinic prohibitions of dyeing see below 22:23.
for you can remove it at once. It can be removed immediately.
and anything whose work does not last on the Sabbath is exempt. For nothing was changed by this work.
the shade of the dye. A tint of color.
kalkantos into gall-nut water. Substances used in making ink (see Hilchot Tefillin 1:4).
astis. A blue dyestuff.
from anything that can be spun. From which threads can be twisted.
one who makes felt. Fabric of wool fibers pressed together.
this is a derivative of spinning. For the purpose of spinning is joining fibers to form one unit.
something from which one can spin etc.. That he make it from an amount of wool from which one can spin such a thread.
medium. Average.

one who makes two meshes is liable. A nir is a kind of weaving (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 7:2). Apparently this refers to knitting, a kind of loose weaving (see Meiri, Shabbat 73a). When he makes two loops in knitting, he is liable.
a net. A woven network.
who wove a bed with ropes. Made a weave of ropes across the bed frame, which is a comfortable surface for lying.
for the threads are first stretched along the length and width of the cloth etc.. The warp threads are threaded on the loom (the weaving frame), and then the threads are stretched and straightened.
one who beats with a rod. Strikes with a stick.
until it is entirely warp without weft. That is, threads parallel to one another.
and when they double it. The warp threads are built of two frames that interlock (are doubled) during weaving, and through them the weft thread is passed.
that he wove at the start. The beginning of the garment.
and wove on the woven fabric. Added to an existing garment.
and if he wove one thread and completed the garment with it, he is liable. For completing the garment is a significant act, even without weaving two threads (see below 11:9).
wove at the edge of the cloth etc.. Special weaving at the edge of the cloth for reinforcement or decoration.
the width of three meshes. The width of three loops made in the knitting work.
a small belt the width of three meshes. A small belt, which has significance even with little weaving.
one who arranges the threads and separates them during weaving. Arranges the threads so the weave will be precise.
the threads. Threads.
one who unravels. Undoes the weaving.
the light garments. Very thin garments which, if torn, are not sewn but mended by weaving.
a knot that is permanent. Fixed, not meant to be undone.
a craftsman's work. A knot specific to professionals.
the camel drivers. Leaders of camels.
the cobblers. Shoemakers.
at the time of making them. At the time of making the sandal, and not meant to be untied.
and a knot that is neither permanent nor a craftsman's work, it is permitted to tie initially. For it is not within the labor of creation, nor does it resemble it.
was cut. Was severed.
an ordinary person's work. A simple person, not a professional.
the openings of the tunic. The edges of his tunic.
even though it has two openings. Although it may be that eventually only one of them will be opened when he wants to take off the tunic.
and the strings of a hairnet. Laces that fasten the head covering.
even though it is loose. And there is no necessity to open the knot to remove the covering.
two ears. Two openings for pouring out liquids, and there is no need to open both knots.

even though she could take out the meat without untying the knot. In all these it is permitted to tie initially, even if it may eventually turn out that the knot is permanent, since at the time of tying it is not a lasting knot (R. Y. Kafih).
with a strap. A strip of cloth that can serve as a garment's tie (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 17:13).
with a belt. A belt.
and we tie a bucket with a strap or a belt and the like. Since he needs them, he will not leave them tied to the bucket.
but not with a rope. Regarding which there is concern that it will be left tied to the bucket, and so he would be making a lasting knot.
and we tie before the animal. A rope across the doorway.
two ropes. Two cords; when he releases the animal he needs to untie only one of them.
and a rope that was tied to the cow, he ties to the trough. Since it was taken from the cow, it will not be left at the trough, and vice versa.
to the trough. A feed vessel placed before the animal.
but he may not bring a rope from inside his house and tie it to the cow and to the trough. For it might stay there permanently.
a weaver's rope. A rope of weavers, in which case there is no concern that he will leave the cow tied with such a rope.

for it is permitted to move it. With the limitations of a vessel used for a forbidden purpose, like all weaving implements (see below 26:1). Some explained this entire law as relating to muktzeh and not the law of tying: that a rope not designated from before the Sabbath is muktzeh and forbidden to move, but if it was tied from before the Sabbath it is not muktzeh, and likewise a weaver's rope (see Maggid Mishneh).
baskets of dates and of dried figs. Baskets woven from palm branches, containing fruit.
he unties, unravels, and cuts. It is permitted to untie the knot that closes it, and also to unravel the weave or cut the vessel to take out the food inside (see also below 23:2).
anything fit for animal fodder may be tied on the Sabbath. For this is not a lasting knot (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 24:5).
his sandal strap broke in a karmelit. Which is a place where carrying is forbidden (see below 14:4, 14:11), and he wants to bring it home.
the strap of a shoe or sandal slipped out. Was pulled from its attachment to the sandal.
most of the foot. The sole.
the bow. A loop knot that can be easily undone although it is tight.
because it is not exchanged with a tying. Therefore the Sages did not decree to forbid it.
