he gathers its two ends, wraps a strap around it and ties a bow. He lays the ends on each other and wraps a strap around both to hold them together, and ties a bow so the wrapping will not unravel.
such as one who ties to measure one of the Torah's measures. For example, to measure a mikveh (see below 24:5).
a harp string that broke. A string that tore.

they tie it in the Temple. Which is not a lasting knot. And although it is a craftsman's knot, they permitted it in this case because they did not decree shevut prohibitions in the Temple (below 21:27).
and he may not tie a string initially. A new string on the harp in place of the one that tore, which is a permanent knot (see Yad Peshutah).
so one is liable for untying it. For untying a knot of this kind.
one who twists. Plaits.
palm leaves. Palm fronds.
the chelef. Sand reed, from which they used to weave baskets and ropes.
this is a derivative of tying. For the purpose of tying is joining threads into one unit (and see above 9:15).
and its measure is enough for the rope to stand by its twist without tying. The measure of liability is making a rope that will be stable and not come apart.
provided he does not intend only to destroy. But intends also to repair by this act.
two stitches. Two passes of the needle through the garment.
and one who pulls a sewing thread on the Sabbath. To tighten the sewing and straighten it.
because it is part of sewing. A stage in the labor of sewing (see above 9:11).

one who tears in order to sew two stitches, in order to sew two stitches. Tore a length of two stitches, with the purpose of sewing two stitches there (for the rabbinic prohibitions of tearing see below 22:24).
one who tears in order to ruin. To spoil the garment, and not for the purpose of sewing it.
in his anger. In his rage.
or over a dead person for whom he must tear. A mourner's tear for one of his relatives (see Hilchot Evel chapter 8, and ibid. 2:1).
for he settles his mind by this and his impulse calms. This is something of benefit, and so he is not merely destroying (see above 8:8 and below 12:1).
and one who opens the neck hole on the Sabbath. Makes an opening in a new garment for the head, which is tearing in order to repair.
with scribes' glue. A paste they used to use for this.
this is a derivative of sewing. For the purpose of sewing is joining pieces of cloth.
and did not intend only to destroy. But also for some repair.
one who levels the ground in a house. Evens out the floor inside a house (regarding a field see above 8:1).
who lowered a mound or filled a ravine. Lowered a raised place, or filled a sunken place.
one who puts the mortar is liable. For a stone does not hold in a building unless it is stuck with mortar around it.
and in the uppermost course. The top row of stones.
for no mortar is placed on it. And so placing is enough to complete the act.
and one who builds on vessels is exempt. For this is not the usual manner of building, and it does not endure.
a permanent tent. That will endure for a long time (for the rabbinic prohibitions of building see below 22:25-33).
one who makes earthenware vessels such as an oven or a barrel. Makes large vessels of clay.
before they are fired. For firing them afterward is forbidden as cooking (above 9:6).
and likewise one who makes cheese is a derivative of building. "For anyone who gathers part to part and sticks everything until they become one body resembles building" (above 7:6).
one who inserts the axe handle into its socket. Attaches the axe's handle to the blade.
one who drives wood into wood. Attaches them to each other.
a chicken coop. A kind of box attached to the ground, with a hole so the chickens can lodge in it.

is liable for building. For so is the way the coop is built (and below 23:1 he wrote that he is liable for striking with a hammer; see the commentators who distinguished between holes and resolved it in various ways).
the door of a pit, of a cistern, or of a loft. These are doors attached to the ground and fixed firmly.
one who demolishes. Takes apart something built.
that he demolish in order to build. So that he is destroying in order to repair (see above 1:18).
in a manner of destruction. In a manner of demolition, which is destruction (ibid. halachah 17).
one blow. A single blow to repair something.
the finishing of a work is a derivative of striking with a hammer. For in finishing the preparation of metal vessels and the like, hammer blows are used.
one who blows glass vessels. This is the work of shaping them, like beating metal.
a shape. For decoration.
and one who scrapes any amount. To repair the vessel.
and any opening that is not made for putting in and taking out etc.. For it is not part of the labor of making the vessel (and see below 23:1, where they decreed to forbid any hole).
one who lances a boil. Pierces a wound with pus.
to widen the mouth of the wound. He wants to make a larger opening.
for this is the physician's work. And therefore it is considered an opening of significance.
the pus. The pus.
one who dresses stone... is liable for striking with a hammer. For it is the work of repairing the stone.
and one who shifts. Moves it to the sides to settle it well in the ground.
is liable for striking with a hammer. For this too is a labor of repair.
nap on garments. Fine threads that stuck to the garment during weaving; this act is repairing the garment.
and provided he is particular about them. That their presence bothers him, and therefore he removes them.
in a casual manner. In an ordinary way.
the white sheen clinging to it. Fine white wool fibers, which appear shiny on the surface of a dark garment.
for the nature of that species is to be trapped. For people customarily trap that species for their use.
to a place not lacking trapping. To an enclosure from which it can be easily taken.
to a tower. A cupboard.
if he chased a bird into a house and locked it in. And the bird can slip from corner to corner, and it is hard to catch even inside the house.
into a large hall. A big hall.
into his cage in which it is held. A special cage for lions, without which one cannot subdue it.
with one bending. One stooping.

until the shadow of both falls to the middle as one. The shadow of each wall reaches the middle of the distance between the walls (and this refers to walls four cubits high (Ritva, Shabbat 106b, and see Lechem Mishneh).
the eight creeping creatures mentioned in the Torah. See above 8:9.
whose species is trapped. For people customarily trap them for use.
even not for a need but to play with them. This is trapping not to use the trapped creature itself but for another benefit, and is defined as a labor that is not needed for itself (see above 1:7).
one who traps a sleeping or blind animal is liable. For to trap them requires effort, and therefore they are not considered already trapped, trapping which is exempt (compare below, halachah 24).
and he was chasing the deer. The person who sent the dogs.
two locked it in, they are exempt. As the law of two who did one labor (above 1:15).
and the second sat and filled it, the second is liable. For the second one blocked the opening with his body.
and the second came and sat beside him. So that when the first stands up, the opening remains blocked.
the first is liable. For blocking the opening before the deer and thus trapping it.
and he is permitted to sit in his place until evening and take the deer. For his action is not forbidden, since the deer was trapped before he came.
one who locks his house to guard it etc.. And did not know a deer was there, and locked the house in good faith; he certainly did nothing forbidden and need not open the door.
a bird entered under his wings. Got trapped by itself in his clothes.

he sits and guards it until dark, and it is permitted. He may remain in his place until the end of the Sabbath so the bird will not escape, and he is not considered trapping, since the bird was trapped by itself.
an elderly, lame, sick or young one is exempt. For they are considered already trapped.
one who releases. Frees from the trap.
domestic animals, beasts and birds. That have already been trapped.
one who traps a beast or bird in his own domain... is exempt. For trapping applies only to wild animals and not to domesticated ones.
chazizin. A kind of cricket.
wasps. Wasps.
since they bite, it is permitted to trap them on the Sabbath. For trapping was permitted to prevent this harm (and see further below 11:4).
and provided he intends to be saved from their bite. That the trapping be done specifically for that purpose (and see above, halachah 21).
one who slaughters. Cut the throat of an animal.
anyone who takes a life. Causes the death of the animal.
by nechirah. Killing by drawing blood without ritual slaughter, such as by stabbing and the like.
one who strangles... this is a derivative of slaughtering. For this labor resembles slaughter in that it causes death.
that dried on it like a sela. Dried on the fish's body to the size of a large coin.
that can no longer live. The fish can no longer survive.
into the animal's womb. Into the uterus.
and pulled out a fetus in its womb. Detached the fetus from its source of life.
that are fruitful and multiply from male and female. Born of sexual reproduction.
that come into being from the earth. Formed from the soil.
that have rotted. That have spoiled and decayed.
one who kills them is exempt. For they are not considered animals at all.
one who picks over his clothes. Removes lice from the garments (see above 5:14).
crushes. Squashes with his fingers.
because they come from sweat. And are not born of male and female, and their life is very slight.
the fly in Egypt etc.. Certain species of these creatures, which are venomous and dangerous.
and a mad dog. A rabid dog.
when they are seen. If they were observed in a place where there are people, even if they have not yet caused harm.
trampled them innocently. Did not refrain from stepping on them if they happened to be in his way.
permitted. For he does not intend it.
one who flays. The hide of an animal that died.
enough to make an amulet. The measure of liability is the size of an amulet, which is the use made of the smallest piece of hide.
for salting is a kind of tanning. It is a certain method of processing hides, and is of the kind of the principal category.
one who smooths. Makes smooth.
one who removes hair... after death. For before death this is not an act of preparing the hide (see above 9:7).

one who separates duchsustos from the parchment. Tanners used for writing to split the hide into two layers by thickness; the inner layer is called duchsustos, and the outer layer is called klaf (see Hilchot Tefillin 1:6-7).
and stretches it. Pulls it taut.
and levels it. Makes it even.
for the cobblers. Shoemakers.
the wing. The wing of a bird.
a derivative of smoothing. Smoothing the hide, making it smooth.
one who spreads a plaster. A bandage, and spreads the medicine over it evenly.
is liable for smoothing. A derivative of smoothing, which resembles smoothing hide.
one who rubs by hand on hide stretched between the posts. Rubs and scrapes it to clean and smooth it.
and provided he intends its length and width and cuts intentionally. That he cuts to a particular measure that he wants.
in a manner of loss. Spoiling the hide.
without intending its measure but like one who is occupied casually or playing, he is exempt. For anyone who cuts a whole hide without the cutting being of benefit is found to be spoiling it.
and one who trims the wing. Cuts off the tip of the feather shaft, to make it a quill for writing.
one who scrapes the ends of cedar beams. Smooths the ends of long beams so that they are even with each other.
a carpenter... a metalworker. One who practices the craft of that material.
and trimmed it to pick his teeth etc.. Cut it and thereby made a useful tool of it.
anything fit for animal fodder etc.. Which are soft.
because they involve no making of vessels. Since the material is not durable, and cutting it is not significant.
and it is permitted to trim spice wood to smell it. He does not cut it to repair the wood as a vessel, but so that its scent will spread.
and strips from them. Separates branches from spice trees that were completely detached from the ground.
two letters. Two letters.
one who erases etc.. For he destroys in order to repair (see above 1:18).
one who writes one large letter equivalent to two is exempt. For one is liable only for writing two letters.
erased one large letter... is liable. For by this erasure he prepared room for two letters.
wrote one letter and completed a book with it is liable. For completing the book is a significant act, even without writing two letters (and see above 9:18).
for his liability is not for the place of the writing but for the writing. The act of writing (unlike erasing) does not concern the writing surface but the writing itself.
ink fell on a book etc.. This erasure is for repairing the book and the notebook.
one letter doubled. The same letter twice, and not two letters different from each other.
one name. A whole word with meaning.
in any script. In any type of writing (font).
and in any language. In any language.
even from two simyonot. Other signs and symbols with meaning, even though they are not read as letters (such as sefirot).
one letter next to writing. Next to letters that were already written.
wrote over writing. That he wrote two letters over letters already written and refreshed them.
and wrote two zayins. Since the letter chet is made of two letters zayin, and he did not connect them.
and similarly with other letters. That he wrote them in two parts and did not connect them, and two letters resulted. He is exempt since he did not intend to write two letters but one.
on the ground. At the floor side.
on the beam. At the ceiling side.
for they are not read together. The two letters cannot be read together, because of the distance.
on two pages of a notebook. Made of rigid boards.
on two walls of a corner. Two walls of a house adjacent to each other.
a gevil. Processed hide used for writing.

for when one brings them together they are read together and no act is needed to bring them near. What is written on two scrolls can be read together if they are placed next to each other, without any additional act, unlike letters on two pages of a notebook and the like, which cannot be read together without cutting them from the notebook.
one letter... from which a whole word is read. Written as an abbreviation, an acronym.
in place of a number. With the meaning of a number, gematria.
one who corrects. Repairs.
and it becomes two zayins is liable. For he is found to have written two letters.
with his left etc.. For this is not the usual way of writing.
with the back of his hand. On the side of the back of his hand.
left-handed. A left-hander.
a child holds the quill and an adult holds his hand and writes, he is liable etc.. For holding the quill in this case is not the main action, but moving the hand for the writing.
with a substance that marks and endures. A material whose writing is stable and lasting (compare Hilchot Gittin 4:1).
and soot. Soot.
and sikra. Red dye.
and komos and kalkantos. Kinds of dyes used to make ink (see above 9:14).
such as hide, parchment, paper and wood. Which are stable materials that last for a long time.
such as liquids and fruit juices. Writing in which fades and is erased in a short time.
on his flesh. Human skin.
because it is skin. A material that endures (above, halachah 15).
even though the warmth of his flesh removes the writing etc.. That is, it is a material considered stable, but the writing is erased due to another cause.
but one who scratches on his flesh the form of writing is exempt. Even if the scratch drew blood, for this is not the way of writing (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 12:4).
and one who marks on skin the shape of writing. Made the form of letters by scratching and the like, and is exempt since this is not the way of writing (an early commentary cited in Yad Peshutah).
one who passes ink over sikra. Black over red, and writing in ink is considered better quality.
one for writing. That he wrote in ink.
and one for erasing. For erasing what was written in sikra, which is lasting writing (above, halachah 15), in order to write in its place.
passed ink over ink etc.. In any case where he did not improve the quality of the writing, it falls under writing over writing, which is exempt (above, halachah 11).
one who marks. Draws.
with kohl and shashar. Kinds of dyes.
one who rules lines. Marks lines on parchment to straighten the writing.
enough to write two letters under that ruling. For they customarily rule the lines to mark the tops of the letters.
for they draw a thread of sikra. They stretch a thread with red dye to mark the sawing line.
the stonecutters. Stone dressers.
so that the stone will split evenly. So that the stone will split in a straight line.
or without dye. But only with a scratch.
any amount. A minimal quantity.
and provided he needs the ashes etc.. On condition that he needs the product of the burning, which is the ash; otherwise he is considered destroying.
and he is like one who tears over his dead etc.. See above 8:8, 10:10.
they are repairers in relation to their evil inclination. They are considered repair in terms of the satisfaction their inclination gets from it.
to temper it. To harden it and make it steel.
this is a derivative of kindling. For its kindling and extinguishing are part of the process of working it (see the next halachah).
but one who extinguishes a metal coal is exempt. For there is no real burning in it.
and it is permitted to extinguish a metal coal in the public domain etc.. For the Sages did not forbid where it removes a hazard (see below 14:11, 21:14).
for loss of property does not override the Sabbath, only loss of lives. It is permitted to extinguish a fire because of danger to human life, but not to save property.
and let them leave the fire to blaze. Let them leave the fire burning.
the whole town. The whole city.
even though they will surely burst and extinguish. Those vessels will break from the heat of the fire, and the water inside them will extinguish the fire.
causing extinguishing is permitted. For this is only an indirect action, not in direct contact with the fire.
and we invert a bowl over the lamp so that it does not take hold of the beam. It is permitted to place a bowl over a lamp to separate the flame from the roof beam, so it will not ignite.
and a tower. A cupboard.
of things that the flame does not ignite. Which are not flammable.
so that the fire will not pass to it. This is not extinguishing but preventing the spread of the fire.
on the board. A board used as a table.
but if he placed it from the eve... it is forbidden to move it. For if it was not forgotten there but placed deliberately, it becomes a base for a forbidden object (below 25:10, 25:17).
we do not say to him extinguish or do not extinguish. We do not ask him to extinguish, but we also do not prevent him if he wanted to extinguish.
because his rest is not our responsibility. Israelites are not commanded to prevent the gentile from desecrating the Sabbath that he wants to desecrate (see also above 6:4).
we do not listen to him. We do not allow him to extinguish.
provided he acts with his father's knowledge. If he acts because he understands that his father benefits from it.
the court is not commanded to separate him. For the court is not commanded to separate from a prohibition one who lacks understanding (Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 17:27).
they permitted saying: whoever extinguishes does not lose. So that gentiles will come and extinguish; only telling them explicitly to extinguish was forbidden.
carrying out from domain to domain. Moving an object from a private domain to a public domain or vice versa (the Sabbath domains will be explained below, chapter 14).

and even though this matter... from Moses at Sinai etc.. Although this prohibition is known through the tradition of the Sages, like all commandments of the Torah, it can nevertheless be learned from the Torah itself.
let them make no more work for the offering of the sanctuary. That they stop bringing their donations to the building of the Tabernacle, because they brought too much.
for the bringing is called work. The transfer of the objects from the individual's possession was called "work" in this verse, and on the Sabbath all work is forbidden (see above 1:1).
from the tradition. In the tradition of the Sages.
from the beginning of four to the end of four. From one end of a four-cubit area to its other end (for the exact measure of the distance see below, halachah 18).
like a useful quantity. Something of a size that can be put to some use (the measures for carrying out in various materials will be detailed below, chapter 18).
and uproot. Lift the object from the ground.
one who throws... or one who hands over is a derivative of carrying out. Because of the similarity to carrying out, although they are done in a different way.
in an unusual way. In a way other than the usual carrying, such as behind him.
one who carries out part of an object. And part of it is still in the domain from which it was lifted.
a basket. A large basket.
full of mustard. Small mustard seeds.

and carried most of it out from this domain to that domain is exempt. Although some seeds completely entered the other domain, the basket binds them into a single unit, and it was not carried out whole.
with coins tied in his garment. In a part of the garment he wraps himself in.
in the manner of those who carry out. For so people customarily carry objects.
even though the load is above ten handbreadths in the public domain. In principle, the public domain does not extend above ten handbreadths (below 14:3).
they shall carry on the shoulder. Carrying on the shoulder is above ten handbreadths. And since that was the case in the Tabernacle, one is liable for it.
and all the labors are learned from the Tabernacle. See above 8:11 and below 13:18.
behind his hand. On the back of his hand.
and the mouth of the pocket downward. The opening of the pocket facing the ground.
in the edge of his garment. The hem of the garment.
a chest and a cupboard. A box or cabinet.
and holds with his hand. Supports the object so that it does not slip and fall.
for so is the way of those who carry out. For people customarily carry heavy objects in this way.

even though he passed it above his head, he is liable. Although above ten handbreadths is not public domain and is considered an exempt place (below 14:3), since the person's body stands in the public domain, the object is considered as having crossed four cubits in the public domain.
for he stands beside them. Adjacent to his place.
and he may. He is permitted.
and they measure for him with his own cubit. By the size of his own cubit, and not by the standard measuring cubit.
he was short in limbs. And his forearm is shorter than usual.
by the average cubit of every person. Average.
and by tradition they said. The tradition of the Sages in interpreting verses.
as it says in the Torah, let each man stay in his place. In the command concerning the prohibition of gathering manna on the Sabbath.
when he stretches his hands and feet. He stretches his arms and legs out in length, for all of this is included in a person's "place."
there were two. Who were in the public domain.
they bring and eat in the middle. They are permitted to carry from the end of the four cubits to the place in between and eat there together.
and the two outer ones are forbidden to each other. For they are not within four cubits.
and to give it to his fellow who is with him within four cubits etc.. This act is permitted, and his fellow carries it another four cubits (and see above 6:22, below 20:7).

because each of them moved only within his own four cubits. This permission applies only when he gives it to his fellow, but it is forbidden for a person himself to carry each time less than four cubits (see below 13:10).
five cubits and three fifths of a cubit. This is the measure of the diagonal of a square whose sides are four cubits.

one who carries... is not liable until he carries beyond five cubits and three fifths of a cubit. For as long as he does not carry this distance, it has not been established that he left the boundary of a four-cubit square.
a place that is four handbreadths by four handbreadths. This is the measure of a place such that if large objects are put on it they stay there (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 1:1).
a person's hand is considered for him like four by four. A person's hand too is considered a place fit for placing an object, since objects can be held in it (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 1:1).
and returned his hand to himself. Brought the object in his hand to the domain in which he is standing.
and intended to carry out the food in his mouth. Intended to carry it to another domain by means of his mouth.
makes it count. Gives it significance.

even though he did not carry out in the manner of those who carry out. For one who carries out in an unusual manner, such as behind his hand, with his foot, in his mouth, or with his elbow, is exempt (above 12:13).
he spat. Spit.
and the mouth of a cubit. The tip of the limb.
exempt. Since it is considered that he lifted and put down in the same domain.
for all the water is as if it is resting on the ground. The water is considered a single unit at rest.
for the fruit did not rest on the ground. But on the water, which is not a resting place for objects.
as we already said. Above 12:9.
both are exempt, because this one lifted and that one put down. As the law of a labor done by two together (see above 1:15).
in what case does this apply. That he is exempt if he lifted and did not put down, or vice versa.
above three. Handbreadths.
it is as if he put it on the ground. For what is near the ground is considered as lying on it (and see below, halachah 16).
and went out with that object. With the same object on him.
until the day ended. Until the end of the Sabbath.
because he lifted and did not put down. His body in the second domain.
he is still exempt. For standing like this is part of walking, and is not considered putting down (see further below, halachah 10).
and likewise one whose bundle was on him and ran with it all day. Similar to the previous halachah, here too he is exempt because there was no putting down (Yad Peshutah).
enough to make a quill. A reed for writing.
that reaches the tips of his fingers. Long enough to reach the beginning of his fingers.
and if it was thick. And is not suitable for making a quill from it.
broken up. Broken.
and they combine with one another. Different spices combine to complete this measure.
a peppercorn. A grain of black pepper.
itran. A flammable liquid extracted by distilling wood, similar to tar.
a good smell. Something that gives off a pleasant smell.
a bad smell. Something that gives off a foul smell.
fine purple. Wool dyed purple.
a rosebud. A closed rose flower (Arukh).
and decayed matter of books and decayed matter of their wrappings. Rot remaining from holy books or from their worn-out wrappings.
because they are put away for genizah (burial). Because of their holiness (see Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 6:8, Hilchot Sefer Torah 10:4).
and one who carries out a flame is exempt. Since a flame has no substance.
that are not eaten by people. That are not fit for human food.
two. He is liable if he carried out two seeds.
gourds. A gourd.

to put at the mouth of a goldsmiths' furnace. It is the goldsmith's practice to throw a little bran at the mouth of the furnace in which gold is refined, so that the state of the metal can be seen (R. Y. Kafah).
for dyeing. Water in which bran was soaked, used in the process of dyeing wool (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesachim 8:1).
a small garment. See below, halachah 8.
tender shoots of thorns. Tips of soft branches.
until they become sweet, a dried fig's amount. Since while they are bitter they are eaten only after pickling, they have the status of human food at the measure of a dried fig (see Yad Peshutah).
and once they become sweet, as much as a kid's mouthful. Since they can be eaten without preparation, and most of their consumption is by animals (Orah veSimchah).
the luf (arum). A tuberous plant that cannot be eaten raw.
those that are pickled. And are not eaten raw.
whether once they have become sweet or before they have become sweet, a dried fig's amount. Since they are always pickled, and are considered human food.
pits. Those eaten by animals.
they are like wood. Above, halachah 4.
and if for calculating. To help with calculation, placing them on an abacus (Toldot Pesach Shabbat, p. 127).
for sprinkling. Of the ashes of the red heifer.
the measure of sprinkling. For the ashes must be sprinkled with a bundle of hyssop; see its measure in Hilchot Parah 11:4.
nutshells etc.. All these are materials used for dyeing.
like a hairnet. A thin head covering.
forty-day-old urine etc.. All these are materials used for laundering (see Hilchot Issurei Biah 9:37).
he carried out soaked dyes. Dyeing materials soaked in water and ready for dyeing.
enough to dye a sample for the weaver. Enough to dye something that will serve as a sample of the garment's color.
the quill. A writing instrument.
letters. Letters.
in an inkwell. A container for ink.
it must contain more than this. Since the quill can pick up only part of the ink in the inkwell (and he is not liable for carrying out the quill and the ink, as explained below, halachah 28).
it is in doubt. Whether they combine.
he carried out two letters. Ink in the amount needed to write two letters.
their writing is their putting down. Since in writing he put the ink down on the paper, it counts as putting down for the purposes of the labor of carrying out, even if it is still moving.
for it has already diminished. Because it dried in the meantime and no longer has enough for writing a letter, so it turns out he did not carry out the amount of two letters.
kohl. A blue substance used as eye makeup and for treating the eyes.
pitch and sulfur, enough to make a hole. With which one plugs a hole in a vessel and makes a smaller hole in the plug.
enough to put over the mouth of a small hole. To plug it.
the shavshevet. A stick with a glue-coated pad at its end, used to take chicks out of the nest (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 8:4).
fat. Fat.
to smear under a coin-sized wafer. An amount sufficient for smearing under a thin, small baked item.
red earth. Red clay (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 8:5).
the seal of a letter. To make from it a seal for closing letters.
enough to make the mouth of a goldsmiths' furnace. To build a frame for the opening of the furnace in which gold is melted.
leek. An edible vegetable (leeks, luf).

clay, enough to make the mouth of a goldsmiths' furnace. Similar to the measure for mud (some read above: "mud enough to make the mouth of a furnace," without the words "of goldsmiths"; accordingly it refers to a furnace for melting other metals, whereas gold is refined at a higher heat, so the frame must be built of clay, which is a more durable material - R. Y. Kafah).
hair, enough to knead into mud. For it is customary to mix hair into mud to strengthen it.
lime, enough to apply to the smallest finger of girls. For with lime they soften and smooth the skin.
enough to cover the blood of a small bird. To fulfill the commandment of covering the blood of slaughter (Hilchot Shechitah 14:13).
a potsherd. A piece of earthenware.
enough to hold a revi'it in it. Liquids in the amount of a revi'it of a log.
a handle for a basket. A handle for gripping the basket.
reed. A bulrush plant that is also used as rope.
a hanger. A loop for hanging.
hutzin. Hard palm leaves.
for an Egyptian basket. A woven basket.
siv (palm fiber). A kind of mesh of fibers that grows around the palm tree.
enough to put over the mouth of a small wine funnel. For filtering out waste matter.
wool scraps. Pieces of raw wool.
like a nut. The size of a nut.
a tarvad. A small spoon.
enough to scrape with it the head of the kadkhed. To sharpen the tip of the kadkhed, which is a wooden embroidery tool.
until it splits two hairs at once. That with it one can cut two threads at once (and this measure equals the measure for scraping the head of the kadkhed - Meiri).
hairs. Hairs.
from the hard hair of a pig. From the stiff hairs of a pig.
wood threads. The fibers in a tree trunk.
palm bark. The branches of the palm tree.
and from kalakh wool. Silk.
and sea animals. The hair of sea animals, such as seals and sea lions.
and all other spun materials. Materials from which threads are spun.
by their measure for impurity. The measure at which they become susceptible to midras impurity (see Hilchot Kelim 27:2).
three by three etc.. Handbreadths.
the hide. A piece of tanned hide.
enough to wrap. To bundle something in it.
it was salted. Processed by soaking in salt.
it was not treated with flour. Not processed and soaked in a mixture with flour, which stabilizes the hide and makes it possible to write on it.
with gallnut. A tanning substance extracted from gallnuts in which the hide is soaked.
klaf. The outer layer of the animal's hide, used for writing tefillin (see Hilchot Tefillin 1:7-8).
the Shema passage. The shortest of the four passages that are placed in the head tefillin.
duksustos. The inner layer of the hide, used for writing mezuzot (ibid.).
the customs-collectors' knot. A sign of exemption from paying the tax.
for it is evidence forever. It serves as evidence afterward as well.
one who carries out a paid bill and erased paper. And it is no longer possible to write on them.
a small flask of paliton. A small bottle of perfume.
and if there is in its blank margin. In the part of that document that is blank.
but a living person is not a burden. Since he himself helps in being carried (see below, 20:4).
leading her son. Guiding him by the hand.
when he lifts one and puts down one. He is able to lift one foot while the other is on the ground. But it is forbidden to drag him if he keeps both feet on the ground.
and a purse. A wallet.

for the purse is not secondary to the child. Although he is exempt for carrying out the child, since a living being carries himself, he is liable for the purse because it is not among a child's clothing (see also below, halachah 28).
with his garments. His clothes.
for everything is secondary to him. For these are his clothing and are not considered a burden.
a live locust of any size. Even the smallest locust, since it is fit for play.
and dead, the amount of a dried fig. For a locust is a pure species and permitted to eat (Hilchot Maachalot Assurot 1:21), and its measure is like that of other human foods.
the vineyard-bird locust. A kind of locust (ibid.).
for they put it away for medicine. It is kept for medical use.
the measure of their impurity is the measure of their carrying out. The measure at which they convey impurity is considered a significant measure for which one is liable for carrying out on Shabbat.
a corpse and a carcass, an olive's bulk. See Hilchot Tumat Met 2:1-2, Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 1:1.
and a creeping animal, a lentil's bulk. See ibid. 4:2.
exactly an olive's bulk. A precise amount, of the flesh of the corpse or carcass.
he has helped by his actions, for the measure was reduced from conveying impurity. He caused there not to be in that place an amount that conveys impurity, and this is a significant act.
but if he carried out half an olive's bulk from an olive's bulk and a half, he is exempt. Since an olive's bulk remains, and it still conveys impurity.
and likewise any similar case among the other kinds of impurity. For only a removal that changes the state of impurity is considered significant.
when he carried out without specification. Without any special intention.
one who sets aside something for sowing or for medicine or for a sample. One who keeps an item for one of these needs is liable for carrying it out in any amount, since he gave it importance.
but other people are liable for it only at its [ordinary] measure. For they do not follow the intention of the one who set it aside.
the one who carried it out threw it into the storehouse. He threw it into a warehouse after carrying it out.
and he brought it in. From there to another place.
he is not liable until he brings in the full measure. For by throwing it he revealed that he no longer keeps it for any particular purpose.
it becomes as if it were burned. As if the first half did not exist.
and he is exempt. Since they did not combine with each other, so it turns out he did not carry out the full measure.
and passed it over the first within three. He passed it over the first half within three handbreadths, even though he did not put it down in that domain.
for one who passes over is like one who put it down on something. See also above, 13:6.
but if he threw it, he is not liable until it comes to rest. As above, 13:16.
in a single lapse of awareness. In one error, without awareness of the prohibition between the two acts of carrying out (and if in two lapses he is exempt, as explained in Hilchot Shegagot 6:8).
to two domains. To two different places that are both public domains, or that are both private domains.

if there is between them a domain for which one is liable, he is exempt. For example, where a private domain separates two public domains or the reverse. He is exempt because those domains are not considered one for the purpose of combining the carrying out.
it swelled and returned to the measure. It puffed up and became the full measure.
it shrank. It contracted.
and he had in mind to sow with it. Before putting it down.
according to his intention at the time of putting down. According to what he had in mind when he put it down, so it turns out there is a measure for which he is liable.
and before putting down he reconsidered and had in mind to eat, he is exempt. Since it does not have the measure for eating, and he is judged by his intention at the time of putting down.

for even had he not had it in mind, he would be liable on account of the intention of carrying out. For in such a case both the first intention and the second are for putting down something that has the measure.
it is in doubt whether it was set aside or not set aside. Since in the middle there was a time of complete exemption, it may have been entirely set aside from liability even if it swelled again.
he threw an olive's bulk of foods. And for carrying it out by itself he is exempt, since the measure for foods is a dried fig's amount.
and it all became the size of an egg. And foods convey impurity at the measure of an egg or more (Hilchot Tumat Ochlin 4:1).

it is in doubt whether he became liable for an olive's bulk because he completed the measure for the matter of impurity. It was not resolved whether we say that since this act is significant for the laws of impurity, it also becomes significant for Shabbat (and see above, halachah 19).
for the vessel is secondary to it. It is nullified relative to the thing placed in it.
he carried out a living person who is not bound. For carrying him out he is exempt (above, halachot 16-17).
the peddlers' basket. A basket of perfume sellers.
even if he carried them out in the palm of his hand. That several kinds were in his hand, and not in the basket.
he is liable for only one. One sin-offering for carrying out all the kinds.
it is a single act of carrying out. It is a single prohibition of carrying out, and anything done in one lapse of awareness combines (see above, 7:7-9).
and a kova and greaves. Of iron, which also serve as protection like armor (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 6:2).
he is exempt. Because he is not liable for clothes he wore. Nevertheless the Sages forbade going out in them on Shabbat.
and an alah and a shield. Shields of various shapes (ibid. 6:4).
he is liable. Because they are a burden.
one does not go out in a nailed sandal. Because of a disaster that occurred on account of a nailed sandal (the incident is brought in the Gemara, Shabbat 60a).
that he nailed to strengthen it. To attach the sole firmly to the straps (but if it is nailed for decoration, it is permitted).

and even on a festival they decreed that one may not go out in it. Since it is a day when people gather, like Shabbat, they decreed this even though on a festival carrying from domain to domain is permitted (Hilchot Yom Tov 1:4).
a seal. A stamp.
and they carried them out not in the way people carry out. In an unusual way, as above, 12:12-14.

because sometimes a man gives his ring to his wife... and it turns out they carried them out in the way they are usually carried out. And for them they are not jewelry but a burden, and so they are liable.
a decree lest she carry it out in the public domain. There is concern that she will remove it from her finger and carry it four cubits in the forbidden manner.
with a threaded needle. A needle with a hole at its end, used for sewing; and it is a woman's practice to go out with a needle with a hole stuck in her garment (Birkat Avraham, sec. 16).
and the man is exempt. Since it is not his way to carry out like this (see below, halachah 21).

and a man who went out with a needle that has no hole is liable. Since it is not jewelry for him, and it is his way to carry out like this when it is stuck in his garment (Birkat Avraham, ibid., and see Yad Peshutah).
because it is among her jewelry. For she places it in her hair as adornment.
a bracelet. A bangle.
and this is so only if it is attached to the flesh and does not slip off. Tight and not loose, so that it will not fall.
lest she remove them at the time of immersion. For she must remove the threads and straps because they are a separation (see Hilchot Mikva'ot 1:12, 2:5-6).
nor with a tzitz. A jewel tied on the forehead.
when they are not sewn to each other. For if they are sewn there is no concern that she will remove them to show them (see below, halachah 10).
nor with the fetters with which girls go out on their feet so that they will not take a large stride. Anklets joined by a chain, so that they will not walk with steps that are too wide.
with a katlah. A gold necklace.
paliton. A kind of perfume.
with a hairpiece etc.. An artificial hairpiece.
with a kavul. A strip of cloth tied on the forehead.
a silver tooth is permitted because it is not noticeable. Since its color resembles the color of teeth.
even in a courtyard that has no eruv. In which they did not join in an "eruv of courtyards," and the Sages forbade carrying objects in it (see Hilchot Eruvin 1:2), even though it is a private domain.
and one who goes out with a flask of paliton that has no perfume at all is liable. Since a flask without perfume is not jewelry but a burden.
of a young girl. With hair threads of a young woman, which have not turned white.
for they are an enhancement to her. For she looks younger in them.
and anything that is woven she may go out with on her head. For the water enters the weave and there is no need to remove it at the time of immersion.
with a diadem. A crown.
with a tzitz and cheek ornaments. See above, halachah 6.
with a hairnet. With a head covering.
with a wad. A piece of wool or the like.
and even if she made a bet yad for it. A handle for gripping.
with the splinters in their ears. Which they stick into the holes in the earlobe.
and with bells. An ornament of small bells (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 6:6).
and with a radid. A garment that covers the whole body.
the paruf. The wrapped one, meaning that its ends are wrapped around something hard.
and if she wrapped it, she may go out in it. Since she carries it along with the cloak and not by itself.
with the splinter in his teeth. To plug a hole in his teeth (Orah veSimchah).
and the one in his sandal. Which serves to join the straps.
and if it fell, he may not put it back. For fear that he will come to carry in the forbidden manner.

for the thread and the cord are important to him and do not help the wound. And therefore they are not nullified relative to the wad and the sponge, and they are considered a burden for which one is liable for carrying out.
and with a bandage. A dressing.
and with an aspelanit, a melugma, and a retiyah. Kinds of ointments and poultices that are spread on bandages and applied to wounds.
and with a sela. A silver coin.
the tzinit. A hard, festering sore.
and with a locust egg and a fox's tooth and a nail from a crucifixion. Which serve as folk remedies for various ailments.

and this is so only if the physicians say that it helps. For if not, these are "ways of the Amorites," which are forbidden as following the practices of the nations (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 6:10, and see Hilchot Avodah Zarah 11:1).
with a tekumah stone. A stone that serves as a remedy for preventing miscarriage.
and with the weight of a tekumah stone. Something that weighs as much as a tekumah stone, which has the same benefit.
with a proven amulet. One whose effectiveness has been demonstrated.
and likewise one who goes out with tefillin is exempt. But it is forbidden to go out with them in the first place, because tefillin are not put on on Shabbat (Hilchot Tefillin 4:10).
one who has a wound on his foot. And cannot put a sandal on it.
he may not go out with a single one. With only one sandal.
with his peg leg. A kind of artificial leg.
wooden ankatmin. A wooden sandal (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 6:8).
for they are not among the usual kinds of clothing. They are not a garment in ordinary use.
with a pikaryon and a tzifah on the heads of those with sores. Pieces of linen and wool placed on sores on the head.
when he dyed them and wrapped them. And thus prepared them for use.
or he went out with them. Walked outside wearing them.
with thick sackcloth and a sagos and a yeri'ah and a chamilah. Kinds of cloth made in a coarse, thick weave.
with a chest. A wooden box.
with a basket. A basket.
and not with a mat because of the rains. For none of these are among the kinds of clothing.
with bells. Small bells.
with a seal of clay on his neck. A mark of slavery made of clay hanging on his neck.
one who wraps himself in his cloak and folded it here and there in his hand or on his shoulder... it is forbidden. Since the folded part does not serve as clothing.
he is liable. By the law of a burden.
with the sudar. A cloth for wrapping the upper part of the body.
and even though no thread is tied to his finger. And there is no concern that the sudar will fall.
a thread. A string.
a short savanit. A kind of towel that does not cover most of the body.
a belt. A girdle.
the fringe. Threads that remain at the end of the cloth after it is woven.
that is not fringed according to law. That its tzitzit are not tied properly, for example where one of the threads was cut off from the start.
because those threads. That hang from it.
a complete tzitzit. A tzitzit tied according to law.
from the adornments of the garment. From its decorations. [Note: Rambam vocalized the word "no'ei" in the Commentary on the Mishnah as "no'i."]
and from its accessories. Something needed for repairing the garment.
the imra. A decoration on the edge of the garment.

for there is no positive commandment without karet that overrides Shabbat. For the positive commandments of an individual that override Shabbat are circumcision and Pesach (each for its own reason), and for both there is a penalty of karet (Yad Peshutah).
with a splinter. A thin piece of wood, which he uses as a ruler.
a weaver. A weaver.
with a piece of cloth. A scrap of wool.
nor a carder. One who combs wool.
with a cord. A measuring thread.
with a sample. Something dyed as a sample.
because he did not carry out in the way people carry out. As above, 12:12-14.
the zav. One who suffers an involuntary discharge from the sexual organ.
in his pouch. A sealed pouch that absorbs the discharge.
even though he needs the carrying out only so that his clothes will not become soiled. For he does not want the discharge or the pouch in themselves, but the side effect of carrying out the pouch.
for a labor that is not needed for itself, one is liable for it. Above, 1:7.
one who finds tefillin on Shabbat in the public domain. And it is necessary to bring them in so that they will not be disgraced.

he puts them on in the usual way. As on a weekday. And although one does not go out with tefillin on Shabbat (above, halachah 14), they permitted it in this case so that they will not be disgraced outside.
he remains with them until nightfall. He stays there until the end of Shabbat.
and if it was in the days of persecution. When the gentiles decreed that the commandments not be observed.
robbers. Bandits.
and carries them less than four cubits at a time. For he is not liable for carrying in this manner (as above, 13:10).
until he brings them to the outer courtyard. A protected place.
but if their straps were not tied, he need not bother with them. For the fact that the straps were not tied raises the suspicion that they were not made as tefillin.
one who finds a Torah scroll. In a place that is not guarded.
and in danger. Since he fears robbers and cannot stay there.
and if rain was falling. And the scroll might be ruined.
he wraps himself in the hide. He wraps himself in the sheets of the scroll.
and covers it again. With a garment.
the scribe. A scribe, whose work is writing.
with his quill. A writing instrument.
lest he forget. That the objects are in his hand, because he is used to them.
since a person is obligated to touch his tefillin at all times. See Hilchot Tefillin 4:14.
until he reaches his home or the study hall. And there he will remove them.
it is forbidden to carry a burden on an animal on Shabbat. To transfer a load on it from domain to domain.
as it says, "so that your ox and your donkey may rest". From this it follows that a person is forbidden to work with an animal on Shabbat.

and the same applies to any domestic animal, wild animal, or bird. All animals are included in this prohibition, and ox and donkey were mentioned as examples of animals that work in a person's service.

because its prohibition comes from the implication of a positive commandment. The prohibition of working with an animal on Shabbat is learned as an inference from the commandment of rest, whereas the penalty of lashes applies only to a prohibition stated explicitly in the form of a "lav" (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:1, 19:3).
the driver. One who leads his animal and urges it on as it walks.

but is there not an explicit lav in the Torah, as it says, "you shall not do" etc.. Is not the prohibition of doing work with an animal explicitly included in a negative commandment? Why then is there no flogging for it?

that he not plow with it or the like of plowing etc.. Here the answer begins (Maggid Mishneh). The prohibition of doing work with an animal includes also labors done by the person and the animal together, such as plowing. Since one who does these labors is liable to stoning, it turns out that the essence of the "lav" refers to a death penalty and does not warn of lashes. Therefore he is exempt from lashes even in cases where he uses the animal in a way that does not carry a death penalty, such as loading a burden on it (for the basis of this law see Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:2).
it is forbidden for a Jew to lend or rent etc.. See also above, 6:16.
a large domestic animal. Large, such as a cow or a donkey.
and he is commanded about the rest of his animal. Even if the owner does not himself do work with it (as above, halachah 1).
and the Sages forbade selling a large animal to a gentile. Although after it is sold it is no longer his and he is no longer commanded about its rest.
lest he lend or rent. For if it is permitted to sell it, he might come also to lend it or rent it.
we fine him up to ten times its value and he takes it back. The Sages obligated him to buy it back from the gentile, even if he is forced to pay ten times its price.
a broken one. An animal whose foreleg or hind leg is broken and which is not fit for work, lest he use it for light work (Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesachim 4:3, Avodah Zarah 1:6).
an agent. A middleman.
for an agent neither rents nor lends. And there is no concern that the animal will be rented or lent to a gentile.
for a horse is only for a person to ride. A horse is meant for riding, and not for labor such as carrying burdens or plowing.

and a living creature carries itself. For it is not considered a burden for the labor of carrying out on Shabbat (as above, 18:16), so it turns out the animal is not used for a labor forbidden on Shabbat by Torah law.
and slaughters it before him. On condition that he actually slaughters it immediately.
and he may not sell it without specification. Not for the purpose of slaughter.
a fattened ox. One that has been fattened, and is certainly intended for eating.
lest he keep it. And not slaughter it immediately.
a small domestic animal. Sheep and goats, which are not working animals. In some places the custom was not to sell them to gentiles, as a precaution because of large animals.
a large wild animal. Large wild animals, which can be used for work.
only through an agent. As the permission for a large domestic animal (above, halachah 3).
one for whom darkness fell on the road. Who was on the way to a city and Shabbat began.
and there was no gentile with him to whom he could give his purse. For the same law applies if there is a gentile there (see above, 6:22).
his purse. His wallet.

until there is neither lifting nor putting down. So that the animal did not lift the object from its place when it began to walk, and did not put it down when it stopped. And there is no liability on Shabbat for transfer without lifting and putting down (above, 13:9, 13:12).
he had with him a deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, and a minor. Who are not obligated in the commandments (see Hilchot Chagigah 2:4).
because they are people of Israel. For in general they were commanded to rest, and therefore he should not give it even to these who are exempt from the commandments.
he gives it to the mentally incompetent person. Who has no understanding at all.

a deaf-mute and a minor, he gives it to whichever of them he wishes. For the minor will in the future reach understanding when he grows up, whereas the deaf-mute could be confused with a wise adult, and therefore neither was ruled superior to the other (see Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 153a).
less than four cubits at a time. For he is not liable for carrying in this manner (above, 13:10).
and even a found object that came into his hand. That he picked up before Shabbat, so that it is his.
but before it came into his hand. If he had not yet picked it up and wants to carry it.
if he can stay there with it until dark, he stays there. He waits there until the end of Shabbat, for they did not permit carrying less than four cubits in such a case in the first place.
with a bit and bridle. A ring with a strap used for guiding the animal.
suitable. Fitting.
such as a sheir. A collar with a ring.
and an afsar. A rope tied at the mouth.
and a chotem. A flat iron strip tied on the cheeks.
for the female camel. A female camel.
and a muzzle for the dog. A guard for the dog's mouth.

for any adequate guarding or lesser guarding is a burden for it. For when it can be guarded with less, it does not need it, and when it is not enough to guard it, it is likewise unnecessary and is considered a burden.
but he may take ropes into his hand. And he can pull several animals together.
provided that no rope extends a handbreadth from under his hand. That it not dangle from his hand more than a handbreadth, lest he appear to be holding a rope not tied to an animal.
and the rope must be... a handbreadth or more above the ground. For if it reaches almost to the ground it looks like a rope being dragged and not like something needed to guard the animal.
with a bell. A small bell.
plugged. Stopped up.
that has no sound. Even though there is no concern regarding making a sound on Shabbat (see below, 23:4).
with the bell on its covering. A bell on its garment.
nor with the seal on its neck. An identification seal hung on its neck.
nor with the strap on its foot. A piece of leather tied on a cracked hoof (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 5:4).
nor with the ladder on its neck. Which prevents the animal from turning its head backward (ibid.).
with a mardaat. A kind of blanket that serves as a saddle for carrying loads.
with the rag hanging from it. A cloth tied to the camel's tail.
unless it was tied to its tail and its hump. Both to its tail and its hump, for it is presumed that in this way it will not fall.
and the camel may not go out with its foreleg bound. Its foreleg bent backward and tied to itself.
nor with its leg bound. Its hind leg tied to its foreleg (Yad Peshutah).
with threads. A marking thread tied to its foot.
with the cart under the tail. So that the tail will not be damaged and torn from dragging on the ground.
with a net. A kind of mesh.
to guard. That is meant to guard the animal.
a goat for which he carved in its horns. He made a groove in its horns, to fasten the halter in it.
she will tear it off. She will detach it.
and bring it in his hand in the public domain. And it turns out he carries four cubits in the public domain in violation.
the males. Rams.
their maleness. Their sexual organ.
so that they will not fall. So that they will not pounce.
and with embroidered rags. Pieces of embroidered cloth.
and the tail. The tail.
wrapped in rags. Wrapped in cloths.
so that the milk will dry up from them. So that their bodies will stop producing milk.

and the horse may not go out with a fox's tail. Which is hung on a horse between its eyes so that the evil eye will not rule over it (Rashi and other early authorities, Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 53a).
nor with a red thread between its eyes. Red wool tied between its eyes.
with the muzzle-bag in its mouth. A vessel with food tied to its mouth.
nor with an amulet that is not proven for animals. An amulet that has not been shown to heal and help an animal, even though it was tested for a person (see above, 19:14).
with a bandage. A dressing.
and with splints. Boards for setting a fracture.
and with the afterbirth dangling from it. An afterbirth hanging from it after giving birth.
and walks it in the courtyard. But not in the public domain (above, halachah 9).
and he may put a mardaat on the donkey on Shabbat and walk it in the courtyard. But not in the public domain (above, halachah 10).

slaves who were circumcised and immersed for the sake of slavery etc.. They underwent a process that is a kind of conversion process, and as a result they are obligated in the commandments that women are obligated in, including observance of Shabbat (see Hilchot Issurei Biah 14:9, Hilchot Chagigah 2:1).
they are like a resident alien. Like a gentile living in the Land of Israel (see Hilchot Issurei Biah 14:7-8, Hilchot Avodah Zarah 10:6).
publicly. In an open and well-known manner.
and we accept a resident alien only when the Jubilee is in force. And in our time the Jubilees have ceased (Hilchot Shemitah veYovel 10:8).

and a righteous convert. A gentile who converted and accepted all the commandments of the Torah, and has the law of a Jew (Hilchot Issurei Biah 12:17; for the process of his conversion see ibid. 14:1-6).

of whom is it said, "and the son of your maidservant and the stranger may be refreshed". Who are the maidservant's son and the stranger mentioned in the verse, whose rest Israel is warned about? For a resident alien and a slave who was not circumcised and immersed are permitted to do labor.
his gleaner. A hired worker for the harvest season.
and his hired worker. A hired worker for a set period.
some matters they forbade because they resemble labors. There is an aspect of similarity between them and the forbidden labors, although they are not among the labors.
a decree lest a stoning offense come from them. For if he acts as he does on weekdays, he might forget that it is Shabbat and do a labor.
whoever levels holes is liable as a plower. Because he improves the ground (above, 8:1). And if he leveled holes in a house, he is liable as a builder (see above, 10:12).

it is forbidden to relieve oneself in a plowed field. It is forbidden to relieve oneself in a plowed field, for there is concern about improving the surface of the ground when he comes to cover his excrement.
one who empties the storehouse on Shabbat etc.. That it was permitted to clear grain out of the storehouse in these cases (below, 26:15), but not to empty it completely.
and he may rub. He may scrub.
and it is permitted to tread on spittle on the ground and walk naturally. For when he walks in his usual way there is no concern about leveling the ground.
women who play. Who were accustomed to play something like this. Children were not mentioned because they are not commanded.
lest they come to level the holes. For the needs of the game.
to sweep the ground. To sweep.
paved with stones. Paved, for in this case there is no concern that he will level holes.
and it is permitted to sprinkle water on the ground etc.. For his intention is that dust not rise, and he does not intend to beautify the ground.
one does not anoint the ground. With oil.
and one does not blow. It is forbidden to blow in order to scatter the dust.
and one does not rinse. It is forbidden to wash the floor.
a courtyard that was spoiled by rainwater etc.. That has mud and water in it, and one needs to place straw there in order to walk on a dry surface.
and a marded. A flattened surface, a platform.
at the bottom of the basket. The base of the basket.
one who waters seeds is liable as a sower. As brought above, 8:2.
it is forbidden to draw water from the well with a pulley. Which helps in drawing it easily.
a decree lest he fill for his garden and for his ruin. To water the garden beds there.
if the well with a pulley was in a courtyard. In which there is no garden or ruin, or from which there is no way to fill for a garden or ruin.
one who uproots is liable as a reaper. As brought above, 8:3.
it is forbidden to extract honey from its hive on Shabbat. For this act is similar to reaping.
a myrtle that is attached, one may smell it... for its fragrance is available. That one can smell it while it is attached, and there is no need to cut it off.
a tree whose roots were high... it is forbidden to sit on them. Because it is forbidden to make use of a tree (above, halachah 6).
and if they are not three handbreadths high, they are like the ground. For up to a height of three handbreadths from the ground, everything is considered ground.
they came from above three to within three. That the root emerged from the tree above three handbreadths from the ground, and slopes down to a place less than three handbreadths high.
even though one side of them is level with the ground. For example, where the ground rises on that side.
or there is a hollow beneath them of three. There is a crevice in the ground beneath the root, but around it they are not higher than three.
a switch to drive it. A branch that will serve as a whip.
and secondary supports are permitted. To lean on something else that is itself leaning on the animal.
he climbed a tree on Shabbat... deliberately, he may not come down. As a penalty, and he must remain there until the end of Shabbat.
how so. They unload the burden from an animal without leaning on it.
a shalif. A sack placed on both sides of the animal.
he puts his head under it and moves it to one side etc.. He pushes with his head one of the sides toward the animal's back, until everything falls off the other side.
he was coming from the road on Friday night and his animal was loaded. And he needs to unload the burden from it.
he takes the vessels that may be moved on Shabbat. He may take the vessels that it is not forbidden to move on Shabbat (see below, chapters 25-26).
and those that may not be moved. Vessels that it is forbidden to move.

for if he wants to pull out the cushion, he pulls it out... and it turns out he did not nullify a vessel. For if the sacks were large and the cushions could not be pulled out from under them, this would count as removing a vessel from its function and would be forbidden (see below, 25:23).
lumps of glass. Raw glass, set aside for melting.
if the sacks were large and full of glass vessels and the like, he unloads gently. For in this case they permitted it, since there is no other way.
he may not leave them there on the animal etc.. He may not leave the load on the animal's back for the duration of Shabbat.
one who sticks fruits together until they become one body is liable as a gatherer. As explained above, 8:5-6.
lest he press them down by hand into the basket. He will push them into the basket forcefully.
and likewise one does not gather salt. To collect it from the places where it forms, even though it is not a product of the soil and the labor of gathering does not apply to it (ibid.).
one who dismantles is liable as a thresher etc.. As brought above, 8:7.
mulberries and pomegranates. For squeezing any fruit on Shabbat other than olives and grapes is not forbidden by Torah law (see above, 8:10).
quinces. Quinces.
and azarur fruits. A small, tart fruit resembling an apple.
because they are not fit for squeezing. They are not suitable for squeezing.
pickled and cooked foods. Foods that were pickled or cooked and absorbed liquids.
if to soften them, it is permitted. To prepare them for eating is permitted, since he does not intend by this squeezing to get the liquid.
and one does not crush snow so that its water flows. For it resembles squeezing fruit.
but he may crush it into the cup etc.. To prepare it for eating.
and the unripe grapes. Grapes that have not ripened.
and the melilot ears. Ears of grain.
if they lack pounding. That they were not crushed as much as needed in the mortar.

to finish grinding the ground grain with the crushing stick. To mash and crumble the pieces of ground wheat with the wooden spoon that is stirred in the pot, since they were ground as much as needed while it was still day.
after taking it off the fire. For it is forbidden to stir in a pot while it is still on the fire (above, 3:11).
one who rubs ears of grain. Separates ears from their husks to get the grain out of them.
he rubs in a changed manner etc.. Because there is a Torah prohibition against threshing ears in the usual way, and the manner of the change is explained below, halachah 17.
one who sucks with his mouth is exempt. As brought above, 8:10, but it is forbidden by rabbinic law.
and if he was groaning. Coughing and having difficulty breathing, whose cure is sucking milk.
he dismantles in an unusual manner. He does the labor not in its usual way.
which flowed. Which ran out.
if they are olives and grapes etc.. For it is forbidden by Torah law to squeeze them, as brought above, halachah 12.
and if they are mulberries and pomegranates etc.. For it is forbidden to squeeze them by rabbinic law.
if he brought them in for eating. He designated those fruits for eating.
and if he brought them in for their press. With the intention of producing a beverage from them.
and liquids came out of them by themselves. On Shabbat.
winnowing and sorting are principal categories of labor. As brought above, 8:11.
although it is permitted to rub etc.. Above, halachah 14.
he blows with one hand with all his strength. He may sort a little of the mixture each time by blowing with his mouth to blow away the husks that are in his hand.
with a kanon... with a tamchui. A tray or bowl, used for sorting and separating (see above, 8:12, Hilchot Yom Tov 3:15).
and one who strains dregs etc.. Strains wine to remove the dregs.
for it is permitted to strain clear wine or clear water through cloths or an Egyptian basket. Since they are fit for drinking without straining (above, 8:14).
and he will come to strain with the strainer. Wine that is not clear.
one who churns. Shakes milk to separate the butter from it.
one who churns is a derivative of sorting. As brought above, 8:11.
he may not churn by hand. He may not separate the lump that stuck together out of the honey.
this is a derivative of grinding. As brought above, 8:15.
green barley. Grain cut before it is fully ripe, meant as animal feed.
for there is no grinding of fruits. In things fit to be eaten raw, since cutting them is not considered processing but the way they are eaten.
and they untie bundles of straw. They loosen the knots of the bundles.
and he separates bundles by hand. He separates the stalks so that the animals can eat from them.
sia, hyssop, and koranit. Fragrant plants that are also fit for human food (and see below, 26:18).
that he brought in as animal feed. And therefore they are not muktzeh (set aside) (but if he brought them in as firewood, they may not be used, below, 26:18).
to pound. To crush, to crumble fine.
he pounds with the handle of the knife and in the bowl. Which is a changed manner, and not in a mortar and the like.
he may grind medicinal ingredients. He may grind kinds of medicines.
he may not eat things that are not the food of healthy people. Foods that are not generally eaten, but only as medicine.
ezovyon and pu'ah. Plants with healing properties.
wormwood. A bitter plant (also used as a spice).
coriander, keshut, and hyssop. Which are used as spices.
chiltit (asafoetida). A pungent plant used as a spice and as a medicine, which is soaked in water or vinegar in order to drink it.

it is permitted to drink it on Shabbat in places where healthy people customarily drink chiltit. For it too is food of healthy people. And because he began this treatment before Shabbat, they permitted him also to perform additional acts in preparing the chiltit, since he might be endangered if he does not continue to drink it even on Shabbat (Orah veSimchah, and see also below, 22:7).

and one may drink Egyptian zeitos. A food made of salt, barley flour, and hairy grains kneaded with water (Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesachim 3:1), which is good as a remedy but is also food of healthy people.
one with pain in his loins may not rub on wine and vinegar etc.. For it is not the way of healthy people to rub with them.
rose oil. Oil perfumed with roses, which is usually used only for medicine.
he may stanch it with wine. To stop the bleeding.
but he may not stanch it with vinegar. For this is a medicinal way.
and if he was delicate, even wine is forbidden. For wine too is helpful as a remedy for a delicate person.
he may not gulp vinegar with them and spit it out. For it is evident that he is gargling the vinegar to treat his teeth.
mastic. Resin of the mastic tree, which is good for medicine and for the breath.
and one may not rub the teeth with medicine on Shabbat. A medicine made specifically for teeth.
the back of the eye. The eyelid.
and fasting spittle. Of a person who has risen and has not yet eaten or spoken much (see Hilchot Issurei Biah 9:38).
even on the back of the eye it is forbidden. For it is used this way only as medicine.
kilor. An eye bandage soaked in a solution of medicines, which looks like washing when he puts it on the back of his eyes.
and he may not press it with his hand to draw blood from it. He may not press on the wound, because of the labor of wounding (see above, 8:7).
hot water. Hot water.
wad. A piece of wool.
and one may place a dry wad on the wound. So that the clothes will not scratch the wound, and this is not considered medicine.
and if it was old, it is forbidden. If the wad had been used, it is considered a poultice, which is forbidden to put on a wound on Shabbat lest he smear (below, halachah 27).
a poultice. A bandage with ointment.
that slid onto a vessel. That fell from his body into a vessel.
they may put it back. Since it is a poultice that slipped from its place.
and if it slid onto the ground, it is forbidden to put it back. Because it resembles putting on a poultice in the first place on Shabbat.
one may wipe the mouth of the wound. Wipe the wound.
lest he smear. The ointment, which is an act forbidden on Shabbat (above, 11:6).
one may anoint and massage the intestines on Shabbat. Rub oil on the stomach and massage.
he must anoint and massage at the same time. Which is a changed manner, for on weekdays one anoints and then massages.
that they press. Squeeze and press.

it is forbidden to stand on the ground of dimoset. The ground of a medicinal bathhouse (or perhaps a place from which hot water springs), and it is forbidden to stand on it, even if he does not bathe or exercise there.
in foul retting water. Water in which flax is soaked, which stinks.
in the Dead Sea. The Salt Sea.
if he did not stay in them. If he bathed and came out immediately it is permitted, since it is not suffering.
even if he has sores on his head. Wounds, which are healed by this bathing.
one may anoint and loosen. Rub oil on the scabs of the sores and scrape them off.
and there is no concern that he will grind medicinal ingredients. For there is no such concern in treating an animal.
to remove the re'i. To remove the excrement.
and it is permitted to invert a cup on the navel on Shabbat to raise it. To place a hot cup upside down on the navel, to bring the intestines up to their place.
and likewise it is permitted to bind and wrap the infant. To wrap him in clothes to set the joints of his limbs.
and to raise the ears. A jaw that was dislocated.
and to raise the unkli. The projection of the xiphoid, the lower end of the breastbone (the "key of the heart"). If the unkli bends inward it can press on the stomach.
for all of these and the like are not done with medicinal ingredients etc.. See also above, 2:10.
sifting is a principal category of labor. As brought above, 8:11.
therefore one does not sift straw with a sieve. To separate it from the chaff.
one who kneads is liable as a kneader. As brought above, 8:16.
parched flour. Flour of grain that was dried in an oven, from which dough cannot be made.
and it is permitted to knead the parched flour little by little. In small quantities.
coarse grinding, for it is like sand. Large grains.
and this is so only if it is soft. A soft batter.
and he must change. The order of adding the ingredients from his weekday habit.
the bran. Coarse bran.
one does not knead it. To mix it with water as animal feed.
and one may put water on the bran and move the tarvad through it etc.. It is permitted to soak it in water and to move a utensil through it in a changed manner, but not to mix it as usual.
even a kor and even two kors. A very large amount.
one may not feed... in the way he feeds on weekdays. In the manner and amount of weekdays, when he is accustomed to stuff and fatten them.
to a place from which they cannot bring it back. That they cannot spit out.
one whose sustenance is his responsibility. That the person is responsible for feeding that animal.
and it is permitted for a person to stand his animal on grass and it eats. Although these are plants attached to the ground, there is no concern that he will pull them up to feed it.
but he may not stand it on something set aside. Muktzeh foods, which are forbidden to move by rabbinic law, and regarding them there is concern that he will take from them to feed his animal.

and he stands before it so that it will turn its face to the muktzeh item and eat from it. It is permitted, with the intention that it eat from there by itself, if the person stands at a slight distance.
removing bread. Taking it out of the oven after baking.
lest he come to bake. For the prohibition of baking see above, 9:1.
he rescues from it food for three meals. For he is permitted to take out of the oven the food for the Shabbat meals (see also above, 3:18).
and he says to others, come and rescue for yourselves. And each of the others too may rescue food for three meals (and see below, 23:24).
the bathhouse attendants. Operators of bathhouses.
even to sweat. From the steam in the bathhouse, without bathing in it.
that he not wash his whole body in hot water. Not to bathe in hot water.
in water heated by fire. That was heated with fire.
but in the hot springs of Tiberias and the like, it is permitted to wash his whole body in them. Which are hot naturally, and there is no reason for a decree about them.
in cold water. Cool water, cold water.
because he warms the water on top of it. He heats it a little.
one who brings a pipe of cold water into hot water. A pipe of cold water that was passed through a reservoir of hot water so that the cold water in the pipe would be heated.
even within the hot springs of Tiberias. For there is no Torah prohibition against cooking in them on Shabbat (above, 9:3).
a jug. A pitcher.
provided they do not heat... until an infant's belly is scalded by them. For heating to this degree is considered cooking.
and one may warm a garment and place it on his intestines on Shabbat. For this is not considered cooking and does not resemble it.
the bathhouse tub etc.. Which holds a large quantity of water (and because its heat is great they decreed about it even though it is not a first vessel - Yad Peshutah, and see the next halachah).
but he may put hot water into a tub of cold water. Because the cold water is greater in quantity.
a kettle from which water was emptied. That was emptied of its water, while the walls of the vessel are still hot.
it is permitted to put cold water into it to warm it slightly. For the water will only be made lukewarm and will not reach the point of cooking.
provided it is not in a first vessel. In the vessel in which they were cooked.
and likewise a boiling pot, even though he took it off the fire, he may not put spices into it. For there are things that cook in a first vessel even after it was taken off the fire.
if he poured the dish from the pot into a bowl. He transferred the dish from the pot in which it was cooked into a bowl.
the chiltit. A pungent plant used as a spice and as a medicine.
one may not soak chiltit, whether in lukewarm or in cold water. For this is the completion of its preparation, and resembles the labor of cooking.
but he may soak it in vinegar. For this is not done on weekdays, and so it does not resemble cooking (Orah veSimchah).
and if he drank it on Thursday and Friday etc.. That he already began this treatment, they permitted him to soak and warm it in a changed manner because of danger.
and he puts it in the sun until it warms. For they did not forbid heating by the sun on Shabbat (below, halachah 9).
it is permitted to soak it in hot water on Shabbat. Since there is no Torah prohibition of cooking something already cooked (see above, 9:3).
one may rinse it in hot water on Shabbat etc.. Wash it with hot water, which is not cooking.

if its rinsing was not the completion of its preparation. For there are things that become fit to eat only by rinsing in hot water, and therefore it is considered a completion of the work, similar to cooking, and is forbidden.
although it is forbidden to heat by a derivative of the sun. Above, 9:3.
for he will not come to err from sun to fire. For there is no concern that one who heats by the sun will mistakenly think it permitted also to heat with fire.
and likewise one may put good water into bad water so that it will cool. To cool drinking water inside cold water that is not fit for drinking.
and one may put a dish into the well so that it will be preserved. In the coolness of the well.
