because he appears to be doing a labor from the labor of the dish. For he prepares seasoning as part of the cooking process.
and likewise he may not make strong salt water. Strong and concentrated.
muryas. Salty brine.
and it is permitted to salt an egg. To sprinkle salt over it and leave it for a while.
but a radish and the like are forbidden etc.. Because it is customary to pickle vegetables.
and one who pickles is forbidden because he is like one who cooks. For this too is an act that makes food fit for eating.
and it is permitted to dip a radish and the like in salt. To dip it in salt, for this is not like pickling pickles.
it is permitted to mix wine, honey, and peppers on Shabbat to eat them. To prepare this mixture for drinking, for it is the way of healthy people to drink it.

but wine, water, and oil of afarsemon are forbidden, for this is not fit for the consumption of healthy people. For it is a drink meant only for medicine, and it is forbidden to drink it and likewise to mix it on Shabbat (see above, 21:20-21).
the next day he strains it. He removes the inferior part from the mixture (see also above, 8:14).
and he may not beat it. He may not mix it forcefully.
shachalayim. A kind of plant used for eating or as a spice (the species of shachalayim eaten today is called "cultivated cress").
and he may not grind. He may not grind them together.
one who removes hair from a person's body is liable as a shearer. As brought above, 9:8.

therefore it is forbidden to wash the hands with something that certainly removes hair. Even though he does not intend to remove the hair it is forbidden, for it is known that it is impossible for that labor not to be done (see above, 1:6).
and it is permitted to scrub the hands with frankincense powder etc.. Cleaning and perfuming materials extracted from these plants, with which it is not certain that the hair will fall out.
with a metal mirror. For with its sharp edges one can cut off hair.
even if it is fixed to the wall. Although in this state it is impossible to remove hairs with it, as law they forbade the use of any metal mirror.
one who launders is liable as a whitener, and one who wrings out a garment is liable because he is laundering. Above, 9:11.
at the mouth of the jar. At the opening of the jug.
lest he come to wringing. While pressing the wet cloth.
and one does not wipe with a sponge. It is forbidden to wipe with it, since water is surely squeezed out of it while wiping.
unless it has a handle. For if it has a handle, it is not certain that it will be squeezed.
with a cloth that is not prepared for it. With a cloth that is not its usual cover, where there is concern that he will wring it out if it gets wet.
a barrel of his was broken on Shabbat. And he wants to transfer its contents to other vessels before they are lost.
provided that he not soak up the wine with a sponge or wipe up the oil. He may not gather the wine or oil with a sponge or cloth.
and he may catch. The wine and oil from the air.
and he may bring close. He brings the vessel close to the side of the first vessel so that the wine and oil will flow from it into it (Ri HaZaken, Shabbat 117b).
a decree lest he bring a vessel through the public domain. Since in his haste to rescue he might forget and bring a vessel through the public domain (for a similar concern see also below, 23:20).
guests happened to come to him. For their needs he was permitted even to add vessels.
and if he used a ruse in this matter. To invite guests whom he did not really intend to invite, so that he could save his barrel.
permitted. For this is a precaution of the Sages only (Beit Yosef).
he rubs it from the inside. He rubs from the inner side of the garment.
but he may not rub it from the outside, a decree lest he launder. Since this act resembles laundering.
and it is permitted to scrape it with the fingernail, and he need not worry that he may whiten it. Since this is not a significant act.
one who rubs the scarf. Rubs it to polish it.
but the shirt is permitted, since his intention is only to soften it. For the shirt is an undergarment, and there is no point in beautifying it.
a shoe or a sandal. Made of leather.
but to launder it is forbidden. To rub its two sides against each other, as is done in laundering.
and one does not scrape shoes or sandals. To remove dirt from them, since it resembles smoothing the surface of the hide, which is forbidden as scraping (above, 11:5).
but one may rub oil on and wipe old ones. But not new shoes, because of tanning (below, 23:10).
a cushion or a pillow that had excrement or filth on it, he wipes it with a rag. And it is forbidden to pour water on it, because of laundering.
and if it was on a leather one etc.. For wetting leather articles is not considered laundering.
with a horse's tail and a cow's tail. With tufts of hair cut from them.
but not with the cloth with which one wipes the hands etc.. Not with an ordinary towel, lest because of the great amount of dirt he launder it.
he dries himself with his towel. It is permitted to dry oneself with a towel.
and likewise one whose garments fell off. His clothes fell into water and got wet (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 22:4).
and he is forbidden to spread them out. To spread them out to dry.
and wherever the Sages forbade because of appearances, it is forbidden even in the innermost rooms. In a place not visible to others, for the Sages made no distinction in their decree.

two ritual pools one above the other etc.. Two mikvehs in each of which there is not the required forty se'ah of water for a valid immersion, with a hole between them that joins them together to the proper measure (see Hilchot Mikva'ot 8:5-7).
the plug. Made of cloth, which plugs the hole between them.

for his intention is that the water should go out. For he does not intend a complete sealing of the hole between the mikvehs, for then they would be disqualified (Yad Peshutah based on Toldot Pesach Shabbat).

and one may plug the drain with cloths etc.. To slow the flow of rainwater into the opening of the drain (the outlet of water from the courtyard), so that it will not collect there and return toward the house.

but one may not plug the drain so that the water goes down to the cistern etc.. To divert the rainwater so that it does not leave the courtyard through the drain but fills the cistern in the courtyard; in this case he wants a complete plugging (Yad Peshutah).
sleeve. A sleeve.
and to fold them in precise folds. To fold them in exact folds.
and likewise one does not fold garments on Shabbat the way it is done on weekdays with clothes after they have been laundered. Which is careful folding.
and if he had no other garment to change into etc.. And he plans to wear that same garment the next day, and wants to keep it from becoming wrinkled.
for it is pressed and soiled immediately. If one does not take care to fold it.
but to fold it in two is forbidden. For it is a good fold, and resembles folding on weekdays.
dyeing is a principal category of labor. As brought above, 9:13.
to apply rouge to her face. To put on makeup.
and sewing is a principal category of labor. As brought above, 10:9.

it is forbidden to fill new pillows and cushions with wool scraps. To put pieces of wool into a mattress or cushion when filling them for the first time, for fear that he will come to sew and close the opening.
tearing is a principal category of labor. As brought above, 10:10.
he separates them carefully and slowly. He separates them cautiously and slowly.
he is not liable for anything, for he did not intend it. See above, 1:6.
and it is permitted to wear new garments. New clothes, although they might tear when he puts them on, if they are not his size.
one may crack a nut in a cloth. It is permitted to wrap a nut in a cloth and strike it until it cracks.
and there is no concern that it may tear. For even if it tore, he does not intend that.
one who drives in a peg is liable as a builder. As brought above, 10:13.
one may not take them. Since the doors of a house are forbidden to move, because they were not prepared for moving (below, 25:6; R. Y. Kafah and Yad Peshutah).
and one may not put them back, a decree lest he drive them in. For it is possible that he will make the attachment of those doors firmly, in the manner of driving in (see above, 10:14).

but the door of a cabinet... one may take them but not put them back. For it is the practice to use the doors of these vessels and there is no prohibition against moving them, but there is the concern that he may drive them in.

and if the lower pivot of them came loose. The pivots are two protrusions fixed in the door above and below it; the lower turns in a hole in the threshold and the upper in a hole in the lintel. Here it refers to a pivot that was pulled out of its attachment to the door.
they press. They push it back into place if it shifted from there.
and in the Temple one may put it back. Even if it fell from the door, for they did not decree a shevut-prohibition in the Temple (above, 21:27).
but the upper pivot that came loose, it is forbidden to put back anywhere. For the upper pivot must be well attached in its place, since the weight of the door does not hold it.
one does not braid... and one does not pokh. Different kinds of hair braiding.

and one may not reassemble a candelabrum of segments or a chair with sections etc.. It is forbidden to assemble furniture made of segments that are made to be taken apart and put together, and join to each other by being pressed tight.

and if he reassembled, he is exempt, for there is no building or demolishing in vessels. In vessels whose normal use involves taking apart and putting together (Yad Peshutah, Orah veSimchah, and see above, 10:13).
and one does not set the vertebrae of a child's spine one beside the other etc.. It is forbidden to straighten a baby's back vertebrae.
one who makes a permanent tent. One that lasts for a long time.
is liable as a builder. As brought above, 10:13.
a temporary tent. A roof made for a short time.
and it is permitted to add a temporary tent. To add a temporary extension to a tent that was made before Shabbat (another version reads: "to add to a temporary tent").
rolled up. Rolled.
the canopy. A fabric hung around a bed as protection from flies and the like.
and it is permitted to place a bed, a chair, and a traskal etc.. For their placement is for the purpose of using them, and not for the purpose of the tent beneath them.
and a traskal. A wide vessel.
any sloping tent whose roof does not have a handbreadth. Sheets spread out that do not form a flat roof but a sloping one.
or within less than three, near its roof, the width of a handbreadth. That even three handbreadths below the roof the sheets of the tent are not a handbreadth apart from each other.
this is a temporary tent. Even if it was made to last for a long time.
a folded cloak. A large sheet of fabric hung from its middle that forms a sloping tent.
it is permitted to stretch it. To stretch out the sheets and enlarge the area of the tent, by the law of adding to a temporary tent.
and likewise the curtain. Which is not made like a roof but as a partition.
a bridegroom's canopy. A narrow, tall canopy hung over a single pole aligned with the middle of the bed.
since it is made for this. Since it is meant for this use, he is not considered to be making a temporary tent in the first place.

provided that it does not hang down from the bed a handbreadth. That the sheet not descend vertically a handbreadth, for we would consider that handbreadth a straight wall, so that the entire slope would count as a roof (see Hilchot Sukkah 4:7).
the plug of the window when it is made for this. Meant and prepared for plugging the window opening.
even though it is not tied and not hung etc.. There is no need for any special attachment of the plug to the window; it is enough that it is meant for this, and there is no building involved.
and it has a surrounding brim so that it makes shade like a tent. A wide rim around the hat.
it is permitted to wear it. For this is not a tent but the fixed structure of the hat.

and if he projected from the garments around his head or in front of his face like a tent etc.. If he wrapped garments around his head so that parts of them form the structure of a roof, and it is rigid, it is a temporary tent.
one who hangs a curtain. Hangs a partition.
that he not make a tent at the time he hangs it. That a space of a handbreadth not be formed beneath it.
if the curtain was large, two people hang it. So that they can be careful during the hanging.
and if it was a canopy that has a roof, one does not stretch it even ten etc.. If one hangs it the way a curtain is hung (R. Y. Kafah), since because of its size even ten people could not be careful.

he may not cover all of it with it, because it becomes a tent. For the cloth is spread across the width of the barrel's opening and forms a tent over it (although with a wooden or metal lid it is permitted, since it does not resemble a tent - Orah veSimchah).
but he may cover part of its mouth. For the contents are not protected by this.
one who strains through an Egyptian basket. Through which it is permitted to strain clear liquids (and not with a strainer, above, 8:14, 21:17).
he may not raise the bottom of the basket a handbreadth above the vessel. For in this case too the basket forms a tent over the vessel.
one who makes a hole that is made for inserting and removing. An opening meant for taking out and putting in.
to let in light and let out vapor. For lighting and ventilation.
he is liable as one who strikes with a hammer. The law of liability for striking with a hammer was brought above, 10:16-18 (and see halachah 14 there).
but one may open an old hole. One that was open in the past and was stopped up.
for if it was below the dregs, it is made to strengthen, and it is forbidden to open it. For in this case opening the hole is considered a new opening.
a stopper. A cover for the opening of a barrel.
but from its side it is forbidden. For this is the usual way of piercing a stopper.
dried figs. Figs.
provided that he does not intend to make a vessel. But only to open it.
for his intention is only to show generosity of heart. And one who cuts off the top of a barrel does not intend to make it a vessel.
it is forbidden to plug any hole. Even if it was not a hole made for inserting and removing.
even with something that does not smear. The prohibition of smearing was brought above, 11:6 and below, halachah 11.

and it is permitted to use a ruse in this matter. So that he appears to be putting food in the hole of the barrel to put it away, though he intends to plug the hole (on the permission of using a ruse for something forbidden by rabbinic law, see also above, 22:16, and Hilchot Yom Tov 7:8).
anything that is the completion of a labor, one is liable for it as one who strikes with a hammer. For in finishing the preparation of metal vessels and the like, hammer blows are used.
one who scrapes. One who planes (above, 10:16).
or on the board one against one, in the manner of singers. An example of a particular rhythm.
or to rattle a nut. To rattle a nut so that it makes a sound.
or to play for him with a bell. To shake a bell for a baby.
one may not clap. By striking on a vessel (Commentary on the Mishnah, Beitzah 5:2).
and one may not slap. Clapping hands.
and to clap with the back of his hand. With the back of his hand.
one may not swim. It is forbidden to swim.
lest he make a swimmers' barrel. A swimming aid, a float.
provided that it has a surrounding rim so that the water will not be drawn out of it. The edge of the pool is raised, and prevents the water from leaving it.
one does not cut a reed tube. To fit it to serve as a pipe through which wine comes out of the barrel.
even though it is not fitted. Made exactly to the size of the hole.
and it is forbidden to place a myrtle leaf and the like in the hole of a barrel. To fold it like a kind of gutter.
and one does not break a potsherd and one does not tear paper. To prepare them for various uses (see also Hilchot Yom Tov 4:8).
a branch tied to a small jug. A long vine branch tied to a small vessel.
one may draw with it on Shabbat. It is permitted to draw water with it.
to scrub. To rub and clean.
with gartekon. A substance used to polish silver vessels.
but one may scrub them with sand and natron. Cleaning materials used for all vessels.
and pots. Pots.
because it is like repairing. Those vessels, and making them fit for use.

unless he rinsed them in order to eat from them at another meal on that same Shabbat. For the Sages did not decree about this because of the needs of the day (Mirkevet HaMishneh; and see also above, 22:22 on the permission to fold a garment for the needs of Shabbat).
and jugs. Pitchers.
for there is no fixed time for drinking. And therefore rinsing cups at any time is for the needs of Shabbat.
but one may spread out [bedding] from Friday night for Shabbat. Since it is for the needs of the day.
because it is like repairing a vessel. By purifying it.
because he appears to be cooling off. It looks as though he is immersing in water to cool down, and it is not evident that he is immersing for purification.
and one may not sprinkle on him on Shabbat. The water of the ashes of the red heifer to purify him from corpse impurity (see also Hilchot Korban Pesach 6:6).
and it is permitted to immerse impure water on Shabbat. And the water is purified by touching the waters of the mikveh.
he puts them in a vessel that does not receive impurity. For if he put them in a vessel that receives impurity, the vessel would become impure and it would be forbidden to immerse it on Shabbat.
such as a stone vessel. Hilchot Kelim 1:6.
and one does not separate terumot and ma'aserot on Shabbat. And see another reason below, halachah 14.
tanning is a principal category of labor. Above, 11:5-6.
therefore a person may not rub oil on his foot while it is inside the shoe. Because it looks as though he is softening the leather.
and rolls. Rolls around.
a ketavulya. A leather mat.
but with old ones it is permitted. For rubbing old leather is not tanning, since it is already soft (see above, 22:18).
one who smears a poultice. One who spreads ointment on a bandage.
is liable as one who smooths. Above, 11:6.
and even with grease one does not plug the hole. Although it does not smear.
writing is a principal category of labor. Above, 11:9-17.
it is forbidden to apply kohl with a brush. To paint color around the eyes.
and it is forbidden to borrow money and to lend money, a decree lest he write. A loan document.
and likewise it is forbidden to buy and sell and rent and hire out. And there is also in this a prohibition on account of "nor finding your own pleasure" (see below, 24:8).
to borrow and to lend an item is permitted. For there is no concern in this that he will come to write.
provided that he does not say to him, lend me. For then it is still considered a loan of an item, although he will return its equivalent.
whether with scales or without scales. Compare Hilchot Yom Tov 4:20.
one does not judge on Shabbat. Lest he write the verdict.
and one does not perform chalitzah. For fear that they will write her a chalitzah document (see Hilchot Yibbum veChalitzah 4:29-30).
and one does not perform levirate marriage. For fear that he will write a ketubah (see ibid. 2:2).
and one does not betroth. A woman (and see Hilchot Ishut 10:14, that it is also forbidden to marry a woman on Shabbat).
and one does not consecrate. An object or animal for the Temple or for the offering of a sacrifice (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot chapter 14, Hilchot Arachin vaCharamin chapters 4-6).
and one does not make valuation-vows. Consecrating a person's value according to the amount set in the Torah (see ibid. chapters 1-3).
and one does not declare cherem. To say that his property is cherem to the Temple or to the priests (see ibid. chapter 6).
because it is like buying and selling. For there is a transfer of ownership to the Temple here.
and also because it is like repairing them on Shabbat. Above, halachah 9.
and one does not tithe animals. To set apart as a tithe each year one out of every ten of his animals (see Hilchot Bechorot chapter 6).
a decree lest he mark with red dye. For in this way every animal that comes out tenth from the pen is marked (ibid. 7:2).
and a person may consecrate his Pesach offering on Shabbat and his festival offering on a festival, for this is the commandment of the day. Since these offerings are fixed for this time.

one does not sanctify the waters of the sin-offering. Which are meant to purify one impure from a corpse, and their sanctification is done by putting ashes of the red heifer into water that was drawn into a vessel (Hilchot Parah 6:1).
if inadvertently, he may eat from what he prepared; if deliberately, he may not eat until the end of Shabbat. See above, halachah 8.
he prepared the fruits. And they are considered tithed.
the demai. Produce of ignorant people regarding which it is not known whether it was tithed, and the Sages instituted to separate tithes from it out of doubt (Hilchot Ma'aser 9:1).
the certain. Produce that is certainly not tithed.
one who designated. He assigned the produce located on a certain side to those terumot, and thereby the produce is prepared.
he may not take them on Shabbat. To give them to a priest or a poor person, for it looks as though he is separating terumot and ma'aserot on Shabbat.

provided that he informs the priest etc.. For if he does not inform them that they are eating from what is meant to be given to them, they will think they are eating from his own, and it turns out that he benefits from terumot and ma'aserot (Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 4:5).
to draw lots and to play with dice. To conduct a lottery and throw dice to win certain things.

and a person may draw lots with his children and the members of his household over a large portion against a small portion. He may conduct a lottery among his family members for portions that are not of equal size.
because they are not particular. And therefore this is not considered buying and selling.
accounts that have no need, it is permitted to calculate them. For there is no concern that he will write.

one who calculates them on Shabbat is like one who calculates them on a weekday. For even on weekdays it is not proper to engage in idle talk (Hilchot De'ot 2:4), but it is not forbidden. In any case one should not engage in excessive idle talk on Shabbat (below, 24:4).
in ordinary documents. Writings that are not holy writings or their commentaries (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 23:2).
his delicacies. Kinds of food prepared for the meal.
but not from the writing. If he wrote before Shabbat the number of guests and portions, it is forbidden to read that on Shabbat.
engraved on the tablet. Carved on a board.
in the script that runs beneath the figure and beneath the likeness. Inscriptions beneath statues.

even to read from the Writings on Shabbat during the time of the study hall is forbidden etc.. It is forbidden to study the section of the Bible called "Ketuvim" at the time set for the sage's lecture (see below, 30:10, Hilchot Yom Tov 6:19), lest he read it and avoid going to the study hall.
to another courtyard in the same alley. That both courtyards opened onto a shared alley.
even if they made an eruv. Those courtyards with each other, by joining alleys, to permit carrying between the courtyards of the alley (see Hilchot Eruvin chapter 1).
a decree lest he extinguish the fire in order to save. And one who extinguishes a fire to save property is liable (above, 12:4).

for he despairs of everything and does not come to extinguishing. Since he knows that he will not be able to bring all his possessions to another courtyard, he reconciles himself to their loss, so there is no concern that he will come to extinguish the fire.
and if they did not make an eruv, he may not save even his food and vessels. Since one may not carry from courtyard to courtyard without an eruv.
three meals. For a person is obligated to eat three meals on Shabbat (below, 30:9).
what is fit for people for people, and what is fit for animals for animals. One may save all the food needed for eating on Shabbat for people and for animals.
and he empties it and fills it a second time. He rescues with one vessel, empties it, and goes back to rescue with it again.
and a round cake of pressed figs. A large lump of dried figs.
and likewise if he spread out his cloak. A large garment, and it is considered rescuing in a single vessel.
he said to others, come and save for yourselves etc.. That he abandoned them and gave others permission to take for themselves, and each one may save for himself food that is fit for him.
and it belongs to the rescuer. For such is the law of one who rescues property that its owners have despaired of (Hilchot Gezelah 6:1-2).
if the rescuer did not wish to take it. That the rescuer did not want to benefit from property its owner abandoned against his will, beyond payment for his effort in saving the property.

and this is not wages for Shabbat, for there is no labor and no prohibition there. This is not considered payment for a full labor on Shabbat, from which it is forbidden to benefit (above, 6:17), since they did not permit doing a labor for this rescue. And since there is no prohibition in the payment itself, it may be paid in the manner of the absorption of permitted wages (above, 6:25), as though it were given in exchange for what was rescued (Orah veSimchah).
fine bread. Superior bread.
he does not go back and rescue bread that is not fine. Since it is evident that there is no Shabbat need for saving such bread.
he goes back and rescues fine bread. Since there is a Shabbat need for saving finer and more valuable bread.
but one does not rescue on Shabbat for Yom Kippur. For food needed at the end of Yom Kippur (when it falls on Sunday), for one does not rescue from Shabbat for another day.
as much as he can. According to his ability.
and it is his, like the food. Above, halachah 24.
all holy writings. Torah scrolls, Prophets, and Writings.
even if they did not make an eruv. And although it is forbidden by rabbinic law to carry there, for the sake of saving holy writings the Sages did not require an eruv for the alley.
provided that the alley has three walls and one side post. As required for the alley to be permitted (above, 17:1-2).
written in Ashurit script. The holy script used for writing Torah scrolls (see Hilchot Tefillin 1:19).
and in the holy language. And not in a translation into a foreign language.
one does not rescue them, even if there was an eruv there. Since it is forbidden to read them, there is no permission to rescue them.

and on a weekday it is forbidden to read them. It appears that this refers to when they are written on parchment, with ruling and ink like all holy writings, and it is forbidden to read them lest they be confused with the valid books (see Orah veSimchah).
he leaves them in the place of destruction. In an unguarded place where they quickly wear out.
and they perish by themselves. But it is forbidden to do an act to destroy them (see Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 6:8).
with sam and with sikra. Kinds of dyes that are not ordinary writing ink.
even though it is not lasting writing. That does not endure over time like ink (see above, 11:15).
the margin of books. The edges that are left without writing (and this refers to those that were cut off from the book or where the book was erased).
the blessings. Writing out the text of the blessings.
and the amulets. Amulets in which verses are written for their protective power.
in which one can gather eighty-five letters from complete words. That most of the book was erased, but complete words remained in it with eighty-five letters or more in all of them together.
and even among them Yegar Sahaduta. Which is Aramaic that is mentioned in the Torah.

a passage that does not have eighty-five letters and has mentions of God's name, such as "And when the ark set out". For in this passage in its entirety there are eighty-five letters, and even if part of it is missing, one rescues the scroll because of the mentions - the names of the Holy One, blessed be He (detailed in Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 6:2) - written in the passage (Maggid Mishneh, and see Orah veSimchah).

and when the ark set out. This passage is considered a book in itself, and therefore the law of regarding it as complete is derived from it (Commentary on the Mishnah, Yadayim 3:5, and see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 9:6).
even though there is money in them. Which is muktzeh (below, 25:6).
to walk about with his affairs on Shabbat. To busy himself with his business matters and dealings.
to inspect his gardens. To tour them.

so that he will not see what they need. This is the explanation why it is forbidden to inspect his fields: so that he will not come to begin examining the needs of the field (in most manuscripts: "it is forbidden for a person to inspect his gardens... so that he will see what they need," and accordingly the prohibition applies specifically when he goes out in advance with the purpose of examining his field's needs).

that he go out on Shabbat to the end of the boundary. That he begin walking before the end of Shabbat up to a distance of two thousand cubits from his place (which is the boundary within which walking is permitted on Shabbat, below, 27:1-2), so that at nightfall he will be closer to his place of business.
when darkness fell upon him at the boundary. He walked to the edge of the Shabbat boundary and waited until dark and Shabbat ended.
attached fruits. To the ground, for which there is a Torah prohibition of detaching on Shabbat.

had there been walls there, it would have been permitted to bring them on Shabbat. For in a private domain it is permitted to move them, and therefore there could be a way to bring those fruits without a prohibition on Shabbat.
for if there were burganin there etc.. Structures attached to a city that extend its boundary (see below, 28:1-2).
a person may say to a laborer, "Do you think you will stay with me this evening?". For this is only an expression of request and suggestion.
but he may not say to him, "Be ready for me this evening". For this wording implies that the matter is agreed and final.
and a person may go down into a pit, a trench, and a cave etc.. It is permitted to enter kinds of water reservoirs in order to drink from them, even if they are very deep and it takes effort.
and it is forbidden to engage in excessive idle talk on Shabbat. See above, 23:18.
such as a mikveh, to know whether it has the required measure. Forty se'ah of water (Hilchot Mikva'ot 4:1).
a garment, to know whether it is susceptible to impurity. See Hilchot Kelim 22:1.
and one may pledge charity for the poor. Set an amount of money to give to the poor.
and even for theaters and gentiles' palaces. For theaters or royal palaces, if there is a public need for this.

it is Shabbat, when one may not cry out, and healing is soon to come. For this is a statement phrased as information and hope, and is not a request for mercy, which is forbidden on Shabbat (see below, 30:12, Responsa of Rambam, no. 208).
provided that he does not mention to him the amount of the purchase. That he not state an exact sum (Maggid Mishneh, and see R. Y. Kafah and Yad Peshutah who explained differently).
one may sail on the Great Sea on Friday for a mitzvah etc.. See below, 30:13, where it is explained.
and one annuls vows. For a father may annul his daughter's vow and a husband his wife's vows (for the laws of annulment see Hilchot Nedarim 11:6 ff.).
whether for the needs of Shabbat or not for the needs of Shabbat. Since a husband and father can annul vows only on the day they heard the vow until nightfall (ibid. 12:15).
and one may ask a sage [for release]. For in various cases there is a possibility of releasing a vow through a sage (see Hilchot Shevuot 6:1).
regarding vows that are for the needs of Shabbat. For example, that they release him from a vow for the purpose of eating and drinking on Shabbat (ibid. 6:6).
even though punishment is a positive commandment. To punish one who was found liable in court (Hilchot Sanhedrin 14:1-2, 15:1).
and the same applies to other punishments. Even if they do not involve a labor forbidden on Shabbat.
and his cucumber fields and his gourd fields. A field of cucumbers and a field of gourds.
he may not clap. He may not clap hands to drive away the animals.
a decree lest he take a stone. A stone or a clod of earth.
and throw it four cubits in the public domain. This prohibition was mentioned above, 14:11.
at twilight. For the definition of this time see above, 5:4.
and this is so only if there is a mitzvah matter or pressing need. See also Hilchot Eruvin 6:9-10.
to climb a tree or to swim on the water. For their prohibition see above, 21:6, 23:5.

he may bring down from the tree or bring out from a karmelit an eruv that he made. Although these acts are forbidden as a shevut-prohibition (see above, 21:6, 14:13), they permitted this so that the Sabbath-boundary eruv he placed would take effect (see Hilchot Eruvin 6:1).

therefore one does not tithe the certain etc.. Tevel produce, which by strict law is subject to terumot and ma'aserot. And although the prohibition of separating them is a shevut-prohibition (see above, 23:9, 23:14), they did not permit it at twilight since there is no pressing need or mitzvah matter involved.

but one may tithe the demai. Produce that must be tithed by rabbinic enactment, out of concern that an ignorant person did not tithe it (Hilchot Ma'aser 9:1). And since its tithing is only because of doubt, they permitted it at twilight (see also above, 23:16).
that he picked from an unperforated flowerpot. And for such picking he is exempt, because it is not its place of growth (above, 8:3), but it is forbidden as a shevut-prohibition.
he carried in a karmelit. The prohibition of carrying in a karmelit is brought above, 14:11.

the court is not commanded to separate him. Since he is not of mature understanding. But his father is commanded to rebuke him and separate him in order to educate him in holiness. This applies when he acts on his own, but it is forbidden to accustom him to desecrating Shabbat, even in matters that are only a shevut-prohibition (Hilchot Maachalot Assurot 17:27-28; and see above, 12:7).
one does not protest against him. One does not protest to the father for having let his son transgress.
and why did they touch this prohibition. What are the reasons for the prohibition of moving muktzeh.
all the more so that moving on Shabbat should not be like moving on a weekday. For the prohibition of moving is more significant for maintaining an atmosphere of rest and cessation on Shabbat.
so that it will not be like a weekday in his eyes. So that he will feel on Shabbat that it is not a weekday.
or to arrange stones. In another version: to put away stones.
and it turns out he did not rest. For there is an obligation to rest on Shabbat even from things that are not labors (above, 20:1).
idlers. Wealthy people who do not work or engage in trade.
and those who sit on street corners. Loafers who sit at the corners of the marketplace.
a rest that is the same for every person. A prohibition that applies to all people.
as will be explained. Below, chapters 25-26.
a vessel whose function is for permitted use etc.. A vessel meant for acts that are permitted on Shabbat.
and an axe for cracking nuts. A hatchet for cracking nuts.
a vessel whose function is for prohibited use etc.. A vessel meant for acts that are forbidden on Shabbat.
for it is forbidden to pound and grind on Shabbat. Above, 8:15.
whether for the sake of the vessel itself. To protect the vessel from being stolen or damaged (below, halachah 4).
or for the sake of its place. That he clears the vessel in order to use the place where it lies (below, halachah 5).
or for the sake of its body. For using the vessel itself (below, halachah 5).
to eat from it. The need of its body.
or to sit in its place. The need of its place.
so that it will not swell. So that it will not swell from the water.

but he may not move it so that it will not break or so that it will not be stolen. For this is moving for the sake of the vessel itself, which is forbidden for a vessel whose function is for prohibited use.
if it has the status of a vessel. That it is defined as a vessel (see below, 26:9).
one may move it. For neither the prohibition nor the permission depends on the weight of the object, but on its definition as a vessel.
the doors of a house... were not prepared for moving. For they are made to remain fixed on their pivots, and are not moved from place to place.
and an eight-month-old living child. Who was born after eight months of pregnancy, and is considered as not viable (see Hilchot Milah 1:13, Hilchot Tumat Met 1:14, Hilchot Avel 1:8).
even not for the sake of its use. For which it was originally intended.
a hammer. A hammer.
a saw. A saw.
a rake for raking dried figs. For collecting dried figs.
the winnowing shovel... the fork. Tools for handling grain on the threshing floor.
the spindle. A spindle, used for spinning.
and the kadkhed. A wooden stick used in weaving.
to poke with it. To stick into fruit and the like (see below, halachah 15).
a sack needle. A large needle used for sewing sacks.
a needle of the whole hand. An ordinary needle used for sewing.
to remove a thorn with it. Which is a permitted act on Shabbat.

if its eye end or its sharp end was removed, one may not move it. Since it is no longer used and has lost its status as a vessel, and whatever is not a vessel is forbidden to move even for the sake of its body (above, halachah 6).
and if it was a golem. That the work of preparing the needle was not completed.
it is permitted to move it. Since sometimes it is left to be used in this state, it is considered a vessel.
of which he is particular, lest their value decrease. He is careful with it lest it lose its value.
such as vessels set aside for merchandise. Vessels meant for sale (even if their function is permitted), and therefore they are not used at all.
muktzeh because of loss of money. Set apart from use out of concern for loss.
the large saw. Used for sawing large trees.
and the plow's peg. The plowshare.
and the butchers' knife. With which butchers cut meat.
and the sandal-makers' blade. A shoemakers' knife.
and the carpenters' adze. A carpenters' hatchet.
and the perfumers' hammer. A hammer for grinding spices.
a vessel that was set aside because of a prohibition. That was set aside from use because of the prohibition involved in moving it.
a lamp that was lit on Shabbat. A vessel that had a wick burning at the time Shabbat began, and it was forbidden to move it lest it go out.
and the lampstand. A vessel meant to serve as a base for lamps.
and a table that had coins on it. Which are forbidden to move because they are not vessels (above, halachah 6).
even if the lamp went out or the coins fell off, it is forbidden to move them. For they became a base for a forbidden item (below, halachah 17).
that which is muktzeh because of repulsiveness. That is not used for other things, because of its repulsiveness.

it is permitted to move them on Shabbat if they are needed. For the needs of his body or place (Mirkevet HaMishneh; and in the view of Yad Peshutah it has the law of a vessel whose function is permitted, which may be moved even for its own sake, and see also Orah veSimchah).
a chest and a cabinet. Cabinets.
whether they were taken apart on Shabbat. For at the time Shabbat began the doors were ready for use as part of the whole vessel.
or were taken apart before Shabbat. Even if they were not attached to the vessel they are considered part of it (Orah veSimchah).
and this is so only if they do some kind of work. They are fit for some work.
a large bowl. A large bowl.
the pach. A small jug.
and this is so only if they have the status of a vessel. That it is evident from its shape that it is made to serve as a cover (Maggid Mishneh).
a handle. A handle.
covers of the ground such as pits and trenches. Covers of water reservoirs.

the cover of the oven etc.. Although the oven is attached to the ground, the law of its cover is like that of vessel covers, since it is not buried in the ground but attached only at its bottom (Maggid Mishneh).
he may not move it with that permitted object. By means of the object that is permitted to be moved.
an unripe fig that was buried in straw. An unripe fig that he buried in straw so that it would ripen.
and a cake. Bread baked on coals.
he sticks the spindle or the kadkhed into them. He sticks a stick (that is not muktzeh, see above, halachah 7) into them in order to lift them.
he may pull them out on Shabbat by their leaf. It is permitted to take them out by their exposed leaves.

he may not move the stone or beam by means of the loaf or the child that is on it. For when he wants to move the forbidden item, he may not do so by means of the things that are permitted to be moved (and they permitted moving in this way only for a corpse, as below, 26:21).
but not a dinar. They did not permit a father to lift on Shabbat his son who is holding a dinar, even if the son yearns for him.
a basket. A basket.

for the stone becomes like a wall. And in such a case it is considered part of the vessel. But otherwise there is no permission to move the stone together with the fruits, rather one must shake it out of the basket, since they permitted indirect moving only when there is no other possibility (Orah veSimchah).
moist fruits. Fresh fruits, which are ruined if they fall and get dirty in the dust.
a barrel on which he forgot a stone on its mouth. And he did not intend for it to be there on Shabbat.
it was among the barrels. And he cannot tilt the barrel so that the stone falls, lest it hit the neighboring barrels.
for they became a base for a forbidden item. And they are muktzeh because of a prohibition and are forbidden for all of Shabbat, as above, halachah 10.
that is in the keruyah. A dried gourd with which water is drawn. And so that it will sink into the water, a stone is put inside it.
if they fill with it and it does not fall. If the stone does not slip out of the gourd while the water is being filled, it is considered part of the vessel and may be moved.
a garment on the reed. A garment hung to dry on a stick.
he pulls it off the reed. And the reed itself is forbidden to move because it is not a vessel.
fruits that are forbidden to eat... are forbidden to move. Because they are not fit for use on Shabbat.
first tithe from which terumah was not taken. From which terumat ma'aser was not separated, and sometimes also terumah gedolah (see Hilchot Terumot 3:13).
impure terumah. Which is forbidden to eat even for priests.
second tithe and hekdesh that were not redeemed properly. For the proper manner of redemption see Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni chapter 4, Hilchot Arachin vaCharamin chapter 7.
the demai. Produce regarding which it is in doubt whether it was tithed, and the Sages required separating terumat ma'aser and second tithe from it.
since it is fit for the poor. For it is permitted to feed demai to the poor even without tithing (Hilchot Ma'aser 10:11).

even though he did not give the fifth. In redeeming second tithe and hekdesh one must add another fifth to the value of the redemption. But giving the fifth does not prevent the produce from becoming ordinary (although by rabbinic law one may not eat the produce before giving the fifth - Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 5:12, Hilchot Arachin vaCharamin 7:3; and see Or Sameach and Orah veSimchah).
even though it is not fit for him. Although one who is not a priest is forbidden to eat terumah, he is permitted to move it, since it is fit for others.

and one may move impure terumah etc.. Impure terumah is forbidden to eat and therefore also to move, but he may move it together with permitted food when there is no possibility of separating them (see also above, halachah 16).
when the impure was at the bottom. And therefore he cannot shake out the impure fruits without dropping the pure ones (some read here "when the pure was at the bottom" - see Kesef Mishneh).
and if he needed the place of the vessel... he moves everything together. For in this case even if the impure is on top there is no benefit in shaking it out, since he needs the place.
a heap of stones. Stones piled one on another.
if they prepared them. If they arranged the stones before Shabbat in order to sit on them on Shabbat.
palm branches that he cut for firewood. Palm branches he cut for use as firewood, which is forbidden to move.
and he changed his mind. He changed his intention.
the straw on the bed. Which is forbidden to move.
but he may shake it with his body. Which is moving in an unusual way, and is permitted.
and likewise if there was a cushion or sheet on it etc.. For it is as though prepared in advance for lying.
if he designated a corner for it. A particular corner in the house, and thereby designated it for his use.
to nullify a vessel from its readiness. To cause a vessel on Shabbat to become forbidden to move, as will be explained.
for the oil in the lamp is forbidden to move. For it is muktzeh because of the prohibition of extinguishing (above, halachah 10, below, 26:14).
therefore one does not place a vessel under a hen to catch its egg. For an egg laid on Shabbat is forbidden to move (Hilchot Yom Tov 1:19-20), and it would make the vessel forbidden to move.
but he may overturn the vessel over it. To protect it from breaking, and although the egg is forbidden to move, it is permitted to move vessels for its sake.
the drip. Dripping rainwater.
he pours it out and repeats. He may empty the vessel and leave it to fill again.

but if it is not fit, one does not place... for one does not make a chamber pot in the first place. For this too is like removing a vessel from its use, and therefore one does not put a vessel under the repulsive drip. But it is permitted to remove the vessel from there, by the law of a chamber pot (below, 26:13).
tevel. Produce from which terumot and ma'aserot have not been separated and which is forbidden to eat, and is therefore also forbidden to move (above, halachah 19).
he brings a vessel and puts it beneath it. To save what spills from the broken barrel.

since if he transgressed and prepared it, it is prepared. For if he separated terumot and ma'aserot on Shabbat, it works to permit the produce for eating, although it is forbidden to do so in the first place (above, 23:9, 23:15). And therefore he is not considered to be nullifying a vessel from its readiness.
to catch sparks. Burning droplets that fall from the lamp.
because they have no substance. For they burn out immediately and do not remain in the vessel, and they do not make it forbidden to move (see also above, 5:13).
a beam that broke etc.. A beam that supports the ceiling, and if it breaks there is concern that the entire ceiling will collapse.
on the length-rails of the bed. The lengthwise rails of the bed.
unless they were loose. That a gap was left between the supporting vessel and the beam, so that it can be removed without the beam collapsing.
and one may spread a mat over stones on Shabbat or over a beehive. Although he is moving for the sake of stones and animals, which are forbidden to move.
provided that he does not intend to trap. For it is forbidden to trap on Shabbat.
to give it sustenance where it is. To feed it in the place where it is.
for he throws it into the cistern, into the water. And therefore he can no longer use it on Shabbat.
because of the suffering of living creatures they did not decree. For a similar law see above, 21:9-10.
and they forbade lifting it with his hand. For living creatures are forbidden to move, by the law of something that is not a vessel (above, halachah 6).
one may not lift. It is forbidden to lift them.
they push. They push.
until they enter. On their own power, into a place where they are kept.
and one may lead calves and foals. One may help young animals walk, without lifting them.
its wings. Its wings.
all the weaver's implements. The weaving tools (for details on the weaving process and the structure of the tools see above, 9:17).
it is permitted to move them like a vessel whose function is for prohibited use. Which may be moved for the sake of their body and place (above, 25:3-7).
except for the upper beam and the lower beam. The upper and lower beams of the loom, between which the warp threads are stretched.
because they cannot be taken since they are fixed. In the space between the upright posts, and they are not meant for moving.
and likewise the weaver's posts. Two large posts standing on the ground.
it is forbidden to move them, lest he fix their holes. The holes in the ground in which they are planted.
date-palm brooms. A broom made from a date cluster (Hilchot Tumat Ochlin 5:20).
for it is permitted to sweep on Shabbat. A floor paved with stones (above, 21:3).

bricks left over from the building are like a vessel whose function is permitted etc.. Although they were meant for building, they are considered permitted vessels since they can also be used for reclining.
for they smooth them and prepare them. For they are smooth and convenient to use.
and if he piled them up etc.. He stood them in a pile, and showed that he designates them for building.
a small potsherd. A broken piece of earthenware that is still fit for some use (see above, 25:12).
it is permitted to move it even in the public domain. Within four cubits, even though no vessel is at hand to cover with it.
a barrel stopper that was shattered. A clay lid that was broken into small pieces.
it and its fragments. The large piece with the small fragments.
and if he threw it to the trash heap. For he removed from it the status of a vessel.
a vessel that was damaged, one may not break off a shard from it. For he would be fixing a vessel for use.
smooth stones. Round ones, which can be used for wiping without scratching.
a handful. The size that the three together fill the hand. And although stones are muktzeh (above, 25:6), the Sages did not decree in this matter.
to crumble. To fall apart, in which there is a concern of grinding (Rabbeinu Chananel, Shabbat 81a).
rain fell on them and they sank into mud. On stones fit for wiping, and one has to pull them out of the mud, and there is a concern of doing a forbidden labor (Rabbeinu Chananel, ibid.).
if their mark is noticeable. If one can still see the sunken stones.
filth. Excrement.
even if it is large. More than a handful.
he had before him a pebble and a potsherd. He had the option of wiping with a stone or a broken piece of earthenware.
he wipes with the pebble. Although the pebble is forbidden to move (above, 25:6), because there is a danger of injury in wiping with sharp vessel shards.
from the rims of vessels. The edge of the vessel, which is smooth and does not injure.
if there were soft grasses, he wipes with them. For wiping with dry grasses is dangerous.
remnants of mats. Pieces that came apart from a woven mat.
pieces of an oven. Which is a large earthenware vessel.
and they are like all vessels whose function is permitted. For with those pieces a permitted labor is done.
lest he drive in. He will attach the leg to the stove (see above, 22:25).
an upper-room ladder. Made like a staircase, which people are not accustomed to move from its place.
and one of a dovecote. A light ladder.
to tilt it. To lean it on another place, without moving it from its place (for more on such a ladder see Hilchot Yom Tov 5:4).
a reed with which olives are harvested. A stick with which the olive tree is beaten.
if it has the status of a vessel. That it is specially fitted to serve for this action.
it is like a vessel whose function is for prohibited use. Which may be moved for the sake of its body and place but not for its own sake.
a reed that the householder prepared to open and lock with. To serve as a bolt for a door.
a door that had a hinge. That was fitted to hang in the doorway.
a muktzeh place. An area with little use.
and it is dragged. On the ground.
chadakim. A bundle of dense thorns.
when they are tied and hanging on the wall. For this shows that they are vessels prepared for moving.

and if they were high above the ground. Hanging so that they do not reach the ground, even though they are not fully attached to the opening (Commentary on the Mishnah, Eruvin 10:8, Mirkevet HaMishneh).
a single board. Not joined from several planks, so that it is not evident from its appearance that it is a vessel and not a random board.
a ken like a threshold. The threshold of the doorway.
a bolt that has a klustra at its head. A rod that serves as a bolt, which has at one end a large circle or the like, by which it is grasped and locked.
it is taken together with its egod. That on the bolt itself there is a clasp by which it is hung on the door.
its egod is fixed in the door. And the bolt is inserted into this egod.
a candelabrum of segments. Made of parts that join to each other.
lest he put it back on Shabbat. If it comes apart, which resembles building (above, 22:26).
chadakim. Grooves for decoration.
that is carried with two hands. Heavy.

if it was large, carried with two hands, it is forbidden to move it etc.. Because it is common for a large candelabrum to be composed of segments, and if people move it they will think it is permitted to move a candelabrum of segments. But a small candelabrum is ordinarily not made of segments, and everyone knows that the grooves in it were made for decoration.
the shoe last. A form on which a shoe is sewn.
a press. Meant to straighten garments or tighten the folds.
they may release. To take the clothes out of it.
but they may not press. For it is forbidden to fix garments, because of laundering (see above, 22:22).
muktzeh because of loss of money. For it is used only for its function, so that it will not be ruined (above, 25:9).
fleeces of wool. Shorn wool, meant for spinning threads.
because he is particular about them. That they not get dirty, and they too are muktzeh because of loss of money.
and the hides. Untanned hides.
and filth. Various kinds of dirt.
if they were in a courtyard where people sit. That their presence bothers those who live there.
spittle on the ground. Which is repulsive, and he wants to have it absorbed into the earth (see above, 21:2).
a kanuna. A vessel in which coals are placed to heat the house.
because of its ashes. Which are repulsive and dirty (Yad Peshutah).
and one does not make a chamber pot in the first place on Shabbat. To cause it to be necessary to move something forbidden for that reason.

oil that came out from under the beam of the olive press on Shabbat. For the beam presses on the ground olives and the oil is drained from them slowly, and it is permitted even though it was not fit for use before Shabbat.
those prepared for merchandise. Those meant for that, and before Shabbat he did not plan to use them.
storehouse. A warehouse.
he begins to draw from it. It is permitted to use the grain even if it was not used before.

for there is no food that is muktzeh on Shabbat at all etc.. For with foods it is not required that they be designated beforehand for use (unlike the law on a festival, where they decreed about muktzeh - Hilchot Yom Tov 1:17-18).
in the muktzeh area. An area meant for drying fruit.
since they rot in the meantime... they are forbidden on Shabbat as muktzeh. For in themselves they are not foods fit for eating on Shabbat.
a barrel that was uncovered and a watermelon that was broken etc.. For it is forbidden to eat them because of the danger of venom from harmful creatures (Hilchot Rotzeach 11:6-8).
he takes them and puts them in a hidden place. For it is permitted to move them because they are food (Orah veSimchah).
an amulet that is not proven. Whose usefulness has not been demonstrated.
even though one does not go out with it. Into the public domain (see above, 19:14).
because it is muktzeh because of a prohibition. For it was forbidden to use the oil at the time Shabbat began, because of the prohibition of extinguishing (see above, halachah 12).
storehouse. A warehouse.
even though it is permitted to draw from it. To take foods from there and use them.
it is forbidden to begin to clear it out except for a mitzvah matter etc.. For one may not move the foods in it unless it is for the needs of Shabbat.
each and every one. Of the people helping to clear out.
four or five baskets. Large baskets, and no more than that.
and they may not sweep the floor of the storehouse. Lest he level holes.
as we have explained. Above, 21:2-3.
and he makes a path with his feet. And thereby clears away what remains, which hinders walking.
the common ones. That people are accustomed to raise.
dry lupine... but not the moist. Which is not eaten even by animals because of its bitterness.
he eats the food. That is around the pit and bones, or under the peels.
and throws them behind him. The peels and bones, and he does not leave them on the table, because he will not be able to clear them from there.
swollen meat. That began to spoil.
and one may move raw meat... because it is fit for a person. For there are people who eat raw meat.
but the unsalted is forbidden to move. Since it is not eaten that way, and animals are not fed with it.
to ostriches. Young ostriches.
the luf. A plant with a tuber and large leaves, which is not fit for people and for most animals when raw, because of toxins in it.
if he prepared them as animal feed. For if he prepared them for that purpose, they have the law of food that is permitted to move.
bundles of sia, hyssop, and koranit. Spice plants (see above, 21:19).
he brought them in as firewood. For use as fuel.
with amita. Mint.
with peigam. Rue, whose leaves are used for food and as a spice.
the fattened one. An ox that is being fattened.
and one does not clear to the sides because of the re'i. To move the food aside so that it does not get dirty in the muck.
and they take from in front of the donkey etc.. Without scraping.
a hanging of fish. A fish that was salted and whose drying was not completed, which stinks, and is similar in this to dried figs and raisins (above, halachah 14, and see Yad Peshutah).
that it is forbidden to move the dead on Shabbat. Above, 25:6.
so that he will wait. So that he will not decay quickly.
cooling vessels. Cold vessels.
so that it will not swell. So that it will not swell up.
and they tie the jaw. Which keeps opening.
not that he raise it, but that it not increase. It is forbidden to raise the jaw back into place, since that would be moving it, but only to prevent further opening.
and one does not close his eyes on Shabbat. One does not close his eyes as is done for a dead person (Hilchot Evel 4:1), for even this slight movement is included in moving a limb.
a corpse lying in the sun. Which is liable to decay soon because of the heat.

he places a loaf or a baby on it and moves it. In this way it was permitted to move a corpse, as though the loaf or baby is the main item and he moves the corpse as secondary to them (see above 25:15).
in any case. In any event, even without a loaf or baby.
because a person is distraught over his dead. And wants to guard him properly; if there were no permitted way to guard him he might transgress a prohibition.
two people come and sit on either side of him etc.. For it was permitted to make a partition for the benefit of the living, but not for the sake of a corpse.
and he is found disgraced among the living, and they are disgraced by him. For they cannot live in their home.
it is permitted to take it out to a karmelit. Even though taking out from a private domain to a karmelit is forbidden by Rabbinic law (above 14:13).

great is human dignity, which overrides a negative commandment of the Torah, namely "you shall not turn aside" etc.. For human dignity overrides Rabbinic prohibitions everywhere, even though there is a Torah commandment to listen to the words of the Sages (see Hilchot Mamrim 1:2; for another application of this rule see Hilchot Kilayim 10:29).
to the boundary of the city. The area surrounding the city.
they transmitted. They passed down by tradition.
twelve mil. About twelve kilometers.
corresponding to the camp of Israel. For such was its length in the wilderness.
two thousand cubits. A mil, about one kilometer.
for two thousand is the open land around the city. The empty area belonging to the city (see Numbers 35:1-5); therefore the Sages ordained that one may go out up to this distance.
it was like Nineveh. Which was "a great city... a three days' journey" (Jonah 3:3).
squared like a squared tablet. Like a square board.
so that he gains the corners. For the boundary then includes a distance greater than two thousand cubits at the corners of the square.
he is given rabbinic lashes for rebelliousness. Lashes by Rabbinic law.
and none of them is four by four. So they are not considered a domain of their own, but an exempt place (see above 14:7).
in a pen in the wilderness, or an enclosure, or a cave. Places surrounded by partitions.
in a valley. In a field.

even if he was asleep when Shabbat began, so that he did not acquire a Shabbat residence. That is, he did not intend to acquire a Shabbat residence in that place (for the way of acquiring a Shabbat residence, see Hilchot Eruvin chapter 7).
two thousand average steps. Medium-sized, for each such step is about a cubit long.
and his measure is completed etc.. His boundary ended within one of these places, which are private domains.
within the city. Inside the city wall.
swallowed up within his two thousand cubits. That is, it lies entirely within his boundary.
and they complete the remainder for him. What is missing from his boundary, from the start of the city up to two thousand cubits, minus four cubits (as will be explained in the next halakhah).
the completion of the two thousand that he has. The completion of two thousand cubits; the city is not counted as four cubits in this case.
in the middle of the city. In the center of the city.
it is permitted to carry throughout the city by throwing. For it is a private domain, and he may transfer objects within it even though he may not walk there.

he may walk in it only two thousand cubits in each direction, even though he is inside the enclosure. For he can rely only on partitions that existed when he acquired his Shabbat residence at the start of Shabbat.

if they enclosed it for the sake of dwelling. For otherwise, it is forbidden to carry in it more than four cubits, like the law of a karpaf larger than a beit se'atayim that was not enclosed for dwelling (above 16:1).
on dry land. On the mainland.

and he may walk all of it and beyond it two thousand cubits in each direction. For he is considered as though he observed Shabbat in the city itself, since he was within its boundary at the onset of Shabbat.
and he slept on the way and did not wake until Shabbat. So it turns out that at the onset of Shabbat he did not acquire a Shabbat residence (see above 5:4).
and when he woke he found himself within the boundary. He discovered that he had slept within the city's boundary, and had not known it before.
for the four cubits that a person has. For one who goes out beyond his boundary, who may walk from his place only four cubits (see below halakhot 12-13).

they begin from the place where he stands. And they are not measured toward the city he left, but in the direction he is going, so that the ability to walk four cubits does not help him return to the boundary from which he left (as below 14; see Orah VeSimchah and Arukh HaShulchan, Orach Chaim 405:3; and see Yad Peshutah, who explained otherwise).
from where his feet stand and outward. Toward the outside of the boundary from which he left.
he may not enter it. For he is not considered to have rested within the city's boundary.
if one foot was inside the boundary and one foot outside the boundary, he may enter. In this case he is regarded as having rested within the city's boundary.
an evil spirit. A fit of madness.
he has only four cubits. That is a space the length of a person with arms and legs stretched out (see above 12:15).
he may walk all of it. The entire area enclosed by partitions.
knowingly. Willingly.
even though he returned unknowingly... he has only four cubits. As a penalty for the transgression.
one who sails. Who goes out to sea.
even though it is outside the boundary in which he rested. For the ship went beyond two thousand cubits from the place it was at the onset of Shabbat.
he may walk the entire ship and carry throughout it. For the entire ship is like his four cubits, since it is surrounded by partitions.
and it was enclosed by a partition on Shabbat. So it is as though he entered unknowingly a pen or enclosure (above halakhah 12).
provided it is not larger than two thousand. For such a partition is of no use regarding Shabbat boundaries (above 5:8).
he enters his boundary. If the perimeter of the partitions brings him back into the boundary.

if he needs to relieve himself, he goes out, moves away, and relieves himself. For the sake of his needs they permitted him to go beyond four cubits, which is a Rabbinic prohibition, out of human dignity (see above 26:23).
and returns to his place. He may even return to those same four cubits that are his place.
since he entered, he may enter, as though he had not left. So he enters by permitted means.
but if he went out knowingly... he has only four cubits. As above, halakhah 13.
with the authorization of the court. By virtue of a halakhic permission.
the witnesses who came to testify about seeing the moon. Who are permitted to go out beyond the boundary on Shabbat on their way to testify (see Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh 3:2-4).
in that place he reached. At the destination.
he is like the people of the city. As though he rested there.
the mitzvah you went out to do has already been done. And there is no need for you to continue going.
he has two thousand cubits from his place in every direction. For the place he reached is considered his Shabbat residence.
and all who go out to save Jewish lives etc.. For they too are commanded to violate Shabbat (see above 2:23).
they return on Shabbat to their places. To the boundary from which they left.
and with their weapons. That they are permitted to carry their weapons on their return as well, so that they will not refrain from coming to rescue another time (ibid.).
that projects out of the city. Juts out beyond the city's borders.
which is the side of a squared beit se'atayim. See above 16:3.
they measure outward from this dwelling house. From that house outward, since it is an attachment to the city and is considered its outermost point on that side.
and so up to a journey of several days. Even if in this way the city's boundary grows very large (see above 27:2).
provided that this dwelling house is four cubits by four cubits or more. For that is the minimum size of a house everywhere in halakhah (see Hilchot Mezuzah 6:2, Hilchot Rotzeach 11:1, and others).
and storehouses. Warehouses.
and watchtowers. Guard booths.
and a cave with a structure over its mouth. A building over the entrance of the cave, through which the whole cave is considered a house.
and a shirayim. Two thirds of a cubit.

and from that projecting house they regard it as though a string is stretched across the entire city. For the house is the outermost point of the city, and from it a straight line is drawn along the whole side of the city, and the boundary is measured from there outward.
even though people live among them. For actual habitation does not make the place count properly as a dwelling.
and the pit, the trench, and the cave. Water reservoirs.
they count both as one city. They consider them connected, and measure their boundary together from the two far ends.
if there were three villages arranged in a triangle. Forming a triangular shape among them.

if there is between the middle one etc.. If the middle one is within the boundary of the two outer ones, it is regarded as though it lies between them on a straight line. If in this situation, given the size of the middle village, the gap between the middle one and the outer ones is less than the distance of the extension for all the villages on each side, the three are considered one city (Maggid Mishneh). Some explained that the size of the middle village is not taken into account, but it is seen as a mere point, and two hundred eighty-three cubits are measured between the two outer ones (Rabbi Y. Kafih and Yad Peshutah).
a city that was enclosed and afterward settled. That was surrounded by a wall before houses were built in it.
from its settlement. From the houses, not from the wall.
elongated. Rectangular.
squared. Square.
four equal angles. Four right angles.
they leave it as it is. They do not square it according to the four directions of the world (below halakhah 7), but measure from its sides as it stands.
they make corners for it. They add corners to it.

so that he gains the corners. The boundary includes a distance greater than two thousand cubits, because of the added corners of the city and because of the squaring of the boundary itself (above 27:2).
they square it. They consider it as though it were enclosed in a square.
he squares it like the square of the world etc.. So that the length of each side of the square faces one of the directions of the world.
and narrow. Thin.
it was made like the letter gamma. Like two sides joined at a right angle (in the shape of the Greek letter gamma).
between its two ends. The two ends that are distant from each other.

they measure for it from the chord. The chord is the string of a bow, and here it means the imaginary line connecting the two ends; in this case, because the boundaries of the two extreme sides are swallowed up within each other, everything is considered one boundary, and the chord is the edge of the city from which measurement goes outward.
a raised area. An elevated surface.
they are measured only from the entrance of their houses. That is, from the place of habitation.
huts. Structures made of woven branches.
they are measured only from the entrance of their houses. And the huts are not combined to be considered a city and squared.
three courtyards of two houses each. That in each courtyard there are two permanent houses.
all of them were made permanent. Even the huts are considered part of the permanent settlement.
with a rope of fifty cubits. A measuring rope about 25 meters long.
and with a flax rope so that it will not stretch further. For if it is made of another material it may stretch, and the measurement would be inexact.
a ravine. A valley.
to swallow it with the measuring rope. To measure the length across it without taking the slopes into account.
provided its depth is less than four thousand. For if it is deeper than that, it is regarded as the end of the permitted walking boundary.
in what case does this apply. That one swallows the slope in less than four thousand cubits.
where the plumb line would descend opposite it, so that it cannot be used. That is, a slope so steep that it is unfit for walking (Arukh HaShulchan).
he does not swallow it. Rather he counts the incline as part of the boundary distance.
unless its depth is two thousand or less. In which case he swallows it with the measuring rope even if it can be used.
if the ravine was crooked. Sloping, and so wide that he cannot swallow it (Orah VeSimchah).
he measures going up and measures going down. He measures the distance as if it were level, not the surface of the terrain (as below halakhah 16).
he goes to a place where he can swallow it and swallows it etc.. At a place parallel to that ravine.
he came to a wall. Whose thickness at the top is not equal to its thickness at the bottom.
we do not say he should bore through the wall. There is no need to bore through it in order to measure it precisely.
he estimates its width. He estimates its thickness, and does not measure it.
and if it can be used. That is, the wall slopes gently.
he measures it with a good measurement. He measures the entire length of the slope of the wall accurately.
and if the plumb line would descend opposite it. That is, the wall was vertical, with no way to use its height.
he measures its width with a good measurement. He measures the thickness of the wall exactly, and does not estimate it.
if there was a mountain that rises ten handbreadths over a length of five cubits. That is, over five cubits of incline it rises ten handbreadths.
and if it was very high. Steep, and therefore harder to swallow.
he estimates it and goes on. He estimates the distance.
if he cannot swallow it. A mountain that rises ten handbreadths over five cubits.
he measures it in small steps. He measures it in small segments, without calculating the slope.

and this is what they meant by "they measure along mountains". This halakhah was said about this matter (unlike the method of measuring that applies in the context of the eglah arufah; see Hilchot Rotzeach 9:4).
the upper one holds part of it opposite his feet etc.. So that the rope is level.
so that those passing by will not see him etc.. For if they see the measurer there they will think he is still within the boundary.
we had established Shabbat boundaries. That were accepted in that city.
they listen to him regarding the boundary he extended. To enlarge the measure of the boundary.

provided that he does not extend more than the diagonal measure of a city. That is, the size of the addition may not exceed the excess of the diagonal's length over two thousand cubits, as will be explained shortly.
perhaps the first one measured the two thousand from the corner of a city's diagonal. And therefore the measure fell short in the middle of the side.

even five hundred eighty, approximately. For if the first measured the diagonal from the corner to be two thousand cubits, the length of the side is a little less than one thousand four hundred twenty cubits.

more than this, they do not listen to him. If the difference is greater than this, we do not attribute it to this difference between the measurements, but there is certainly an error here, and we rely on the established boundaries.

even a slave, even a maidservant, are trusted to say "up to here is the Shabbat boundary". Even though they are generally disqualified from testifying (see Hilchot Edut chapter 9), the Sages relied on their words in a case of need (see Hilchot Gerushin 12:15).
and an adult is trusted etc.. We accept the testimony of an adult about what happened in his childhood in matters of Rabbinic law (see Hilchot Edut 14:3).
to sanctify the Shabbat day with words. To recite the text of blessings dealing with the distinctiveness and holiness of the day.
remember it with a remembrance of praise and sanctification. And this remembrance is by speech.
the Kiddush of the day. Recited at the onset of Shabbat.
a remembrance of the work of Creation. Like the Holy One's resting on the seventh day of Creation.
first among the holy convocations. Shabbat is mentioned at the head of the list of the Lord's sanctified appointed times, which also includes all the festivals (see Leviticus chapter 23).
a remembrance of the exodus from Egypt. For even remembering the slavery in Egypt and the departure from there is a reason for the mitzvah of Shabbat (see Deuteronomy 5:14).
for You chose us and sanctified us from all the nations etc.. For the mitzvah of Shabbat was given to Israel alone (Exodus 31:17; and see Hilchot Melachim 10:9).
who distinguishes between holy and profane. See Leviticus 10:10.
and between light and darkness. See Genesis 1:4.
and between Israel and the nations. See Leviticus 20:26.
the main Kiddush is at night. Close to the onset of Shabbat (see below halakhah 11).
but only at the end of Shabbat. For that was when fire was first created by man (below halakhah 27).
once the day has become sanctified. From the onset of Shabbat.
he is forbidden to begin etc.. But if he began while it was still day, he need not stop (see below halakhah 12).
by Rabbinic law, to recite Kiddush over wine and Havdalah over wine. The Sages ordained that the recitation of the words of remembrance be done in conjunction with the blessing over a cup of wine.
for he made Havdalah in the prayer. In the blessing "Atah Chonen" (see Seder HaTefillot, blessings of the Amidah, 3).
and he says "who distinguishes between holy and profane". Even without the blessing formula.
a revi'it. A quarter of a log (for its measure see the opinions and views).
and he rinses it inside and washes it outside. For this is the respectful way, that the cup be clean (see also Hilchot Berakhot 7:15).
and it is a widespread custom. Common.
and they were completed. Which tells of the Creator's resting on the seventh day from the work of Creation (Genesis 2:1-3).
a mouthful. His mouthful (see Hilchot Shevitat Asor 2:1).
in the place of a meal. In the very place where the meal will be eaten.
in a corner. A corner of the house.

and why do we recite Kiddush in the synagogue. For since ancient generations it was the custom that the cantor recites Kiddush in the synagogue after the Friday night evening prayer, even though the worshippers eat in their homes.
because of the guests who eat and drink there. And for them it is a place of a meal.
and he blesses "hamotzi" and sanctifies. For one may recite Kiddush over bread as well.
breaks. Cuts.
he sanctifies over the bread and does not sanctify over wine. In order to place the blessing over bread right next to the washing of hands.
and it is a mitzvah to bless over wine on the Shabbat day before he eats the second meal. Out of honor for the day.
Kiddusha Rabba. The great Kiddush (for the meaning of the name see the commentators on Babylonian Talmud Pesachim 106a).
and a person is forbidden to taste anything etc.. As with the night Kiddush (above halakhah 5).
and this Kiddush too must be only in the place of a meal. As above, halakhah 8.
a person may. Is permitted.
and likewise he makes Havdalah over the cup while it is still day. Without blessing over the candle, since it is still forbidden to do work until Shabbat ends.
either a little before this hour. For this mitzvah has no precise time.
he spreads a cloth over the table. Which is a kind of break in the meal and a new beginning in honor of Shabbat.
if he was eating on Shabbat and Shabbat ended... he finishes his meal. For there is no need to interrupt his meal for Havdalah.
and washes his hands. With the final waters (see Hilchot Berakhot 6:1-2).
and recites Birkat HaMazon over the cup. See Hilchot Berakhot 7:15.
and if he was in the middle of drinking, he stops. For reclining to drink does not count as establishing a meal.
and he finishes his eating with the onset of Shabbat. And he does not want to eat any more.
over a second cup. Another cup, not the one used for Birkat HaMazon.
for one does not perform two mitzvot with one cup. For it looks as though he wants to be rid of the mitzvot and finish them quickly.

they are Torah mitzvot. Above halakhah 1, Hilchot Berakhot 1:1 (and the commentators discussed the difference between Kiddush and Havdalah; see Maggid Mishneh, Yad Peshutah, Rabbi Y. Kafih and others).
wine fit for pouring on the altar. Wine that has not changed from its nature (see Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 6:9-10).
honey or leaven. Which are forbidden for burning on the altar (ibid. 5:1-4).
