and so we rule in all the West. The countries of North Africa, and possibly including Spain (see also Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 11:9-10).
and there are those who permit Kiddush over it etc.. That is, it is not truly spoiled wine, but is disqualified for libation because of some other prohibition.
uncovered. A drink left in an open vessel, with concern that a venomous creature may have drunk from it (see Hilchot Rotzeach 11:6-16).
whose taste is the taste of vinegar etc.. For it is no longer in the category of wine.
lees. The sediment of wine.
on which he poured water. In order to extract the remaining wine from them.

where he poured three of water on the lees and drew out less than four etc.. That is, the liquid that came out of the lees exceeded the water put in only slightly. But if a large quantity of liquid came out, up to an additional measure beyond the three that were put in, it is judged as diluted wine (for the maximum dilution is three measures of water to one of wine), and the additional measure that came out is regarded as wine that drained from the lees (see also Hilchot Berakhot 8:9).
this is its disqualification... because it is like the leftovers of cups. And it is not respectful to recite Kiddush over it.
and its taste is the taste of wine, one may recite Kiddush over it. For it has the status of wine.
diluted wine. Mixed with water.
new wine from its vat. Before it has fermented sufficiently.
at its time. Immediately after it was pressed.
a country where most of its wine is shekhar. Where in place of wine they use shekhar made from other fruits.
the wine of the country. It is regarded as wine with respect to that place.

for they are all "Sabbaths of the Lord". For this expression was expounded as referring to all festival days (see Torat Kohanim, Emor, parashah 12, halakhah 6), so that the mitzvah of sanctifying Shabbat (mentioned above in halakhah 1) applies to them as well.
but one does not make Havdalah at the end of a festival that falls before Shabbat. For the holiness of Shabbat is greater.
and exalted us above every tongue. Made us superior to all the nations.
and the times. The festivals.
in the way he concludes in the prayer. In the middle blessing of the Amidah (see Seder HaTefillot, middle blessings on Shabbat and festivals, 10).
this day of remembrance, a remembrance of the shofar blast. See Leviticus 23:24.
on the night of a festival that falls on Sunday. For the festival enters as Shabbat ends, and Havdalah is needed in honor of the end of Shabbat, and Kiddush in honor of the festival that is entering.
he blesses over the candle. As below, halakhah 24.
for it is not a festival in its own right. Rather it is a continuation of the festival of Passover.
until they can benefit from its light etc.. They make use of the light it gives, to the extent that one can see things clearly by it.
whose ordinary use is for idolatry. And one does not bless over benefiting from something forbidden (compare Hilchot Berakhot 9:7-9).
nor over the candle of the dead. Which is not made to give light, but to honor the dead (see ibid.).
a Jew who lit from a gentile, or a gentile from a Jew, one blesses over it. For this is not included in the candle of gentiles.
to a kerakh. A large city, in which there are Jews and gentiles.
the fire of a kiln, of an oven, and of a stove. For it was made not for light but for heat.
the coals. Whose fire is not apparent.
the fire of the study hall etc.. Which is lit in honor of the study hall or in honor of the synagogue.
and a torch. A brand, a large fire.

fire that was lit on Shabbat for a sick person or a woman after childbirth. For they lit a fire for their needs, and this is permitted because of saving life (see above chapter 2). But one does not bless over fire that was lit on Shabbat in violation.
fire that was kindled etc.. Fire that was kindled at the end of Shabbat and was not burning during Shabbat.
for it was the beginning of its creation by man. For the first fire was created by man at the end of Shabbat (see Babylonian Talmud Berakhot 54a, Jerusalem Talmud ibid. 8:5).

for at the end of Yom Kippur one blesses only over fire that rested. That was burning throughout Yom Kippur and was not used in a transgression. And one blesses over it at the end of Yom Kippur, when lighting fire is again permitted. And with newly lit fire this is not apparent.

even though it was lit for a sick person... for it rested from transgression. Even though the candle was lit on Yom Kippur itself, it is regarded as a "candle that rested," for no transgression was committed in lighting it.
in the middle of Shabbat. On one of the weekdays.

and between the seventh day and the six days of work... for the order of distinctions enumerates. Even though the distinguishing of the seventh day does not apply to that day, this is the text of Havdalah, which lists various distinctions.

and not over the candle. For the reason of the creation of fire at the end of Shabbat does not apply, nor the reason for blessing at the end of Yom Kippur, since on a festival the work of kindling was permitted (see Hilchot Yom Tov 1:4).
sorrowful. Sad.
four things were said about Shabbat. Central matters.
remember. In Kiddush and Havdalah (above chapter 29).
and observe. In the prohibitions of labors.
honor and delight. To be explained in this chapter.
in hot water. In warm water.
and wraps himself in tzitzit. Wears a tallit with tzitzit, which is a special and honorable garment.
waits eagerly. Looks forward.
a clean garment. A clean cloak.
and his weekday clothing should not be like his Shabbat clothing. For he must have other, special clothes for Shabbat.
he lets his tallit hang down. He unfolds the tallit and wears it spread out, which is a respectful way (see Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 8:4).
so that his clothing will not be like weekday clothing. For on weekdays people fold and lift the tallit off the ground so it will not get dirty while working (see also Hilchot De'ot 5:9).
that the people should do laundry on Thursday. So that the clothes will be clean and ready in honor of Shabbat.
to establish a meal and a drinking feast. A festive and special meal.
and it is permitted to eat and drink until dark. For there is no prohibition against an ordinary meal.
from Minchah onward. From two and a half hours before sunset onward.
a person arranges his table. Sets it for a meal.
for he needs only an olive's bulk. That is, he is not hungry and does not intend to eat much.
he arranges his table at the end of Shabbat. For a meal in honor of the departure of Shabbat.
to prepare his house while it is still day. To arrange and ready it.
and it is not his way to buy. He is not accustomed to buy by himself, as a matter of his dignity.
personally. Himself.
braids. Weaves.
very rich stew and spiced drink. Fine foods.
a boiled vegetable. Cooked greens.
to be pinched for himself and to borrow from others. To strain his situation and to ask for a loan or a gift.
for all his days are like Shabbat. That even on weekdays he eats fine foods.
to make the Shabbat food differ from the weekday food. That the food be special for Shabbat.
he changes the time of eating. So that it will be evident that this is a special meal.
ill from too much eating. For eating harms his body.
or who was fasting. Who was accustomed to fast, and therefore it is hard for him to eat much.
to establish each of the three meals over wine. To bless over the wine before the meal (see also Hilchot Berakhot 4:12).
whose means suffice. Whose financial situation allows it.
at the time of the study hall. At the time when the people gather for the sermon.
he reads and listens. He studies Torah.
more than three parsa'ot. About twelve kilometers.
and the day is still long, and he can prepare a Shabbat meal. That he arrives when there is still plenty of time, enough to prepare his meal.
for he embarrasses them. If he arrives at an hour when they will not have time to prepare things in his honor.

in a trouble among the troubles for which the community fasts and sounds the alarm. For the community is commanded to cry out and sound the trumpets over every trouble that comes (Hilchot Ta'aniyot 1:1; for details of the troubles for which they fast see ibid. chapter 2).
one does not fast or sound the alarm on Shabbat or on festivals. For fast days and prayer days are not established on them (ibid. 1:6).
for whom they sound the alarm on Shabbat to help them. They blow trumpets to summon whoever can rescue them.
and they plead and ask for mercy for them. Because their situation is dangerous (see also above 2:24).
besieging. Laying siege (see also above 2:25).

and stipulates with him to rest and he does not rest. He agrees in advance with the gentile who steers the ship that he will refrain from work on Shabbat. And even if in the end he does not rest, it is of no consequence (see also above 24:6).
and from Tyre to Sidon. For this is not a long voyage.
